          The ordinary-double-point gap in every dimension
                                            OpenAI

                                     September 24, 2026


                                            Abstract
         We prove the ordinary-double-point gap conjecture for boundary-zero complex alge-
      braic klt germs in every dimension: a singular n-dimensional germ has normalized volume
      at most 2(n − 1)n , with equality precisely at an analytic ordinary double point.

1    Introduction
Normalized volume, introduced by Chi Li [26], measures the size of a klt singularity by
balancing the discrepancy of a valuation against the asymptotic colength of its valuation
ideals. For a closed point x of an n-dimensional normal complex variety that is klt near x,
with zero boundary, it is

                           vol(x,
                           ˆ      X) =        inf          AX (v)n vol(v).
                                         v centered at x

Here AX (v) is log discrepancy, and vol(v) is the leading colength of the ideals {f : v(f ) ≥ t},
multiplied by n!. Section 2 gives the precise conventions for real valuations, including infinite
discrepancy. In dimension n, the largest normalized volume is nn , attained exactly at smooth
points [36, Theorem 1.6]. The ordinary double point gap conjecture predicts the next largest
value: every singular klt germ should have normalized volume at most 2(n − 1)n , and this
value should characterize the ordinary double point. Besides distinguishing a basic singularity
by a numerical invariant, such a gap gives global restrictions on K-semistable Fano varieties
through the local-to-global volume inequality [33, Theorem 21].
    An ordinary double point is the analytic hypersurface germ of a nondegenerate quadratic
form. It is the simplest singular quadratic cone, and the asserted gap concerns all singular klt
germs, not only hypersurfaces. Thus an essential part of the problem is to extract structural
information from a numerical lower bound on volume.




                                                 2
Theorem 1.1 (The ordinary double point gap). Let n ≥ 2, and let x be a singular closed
point of a normal complex algebraic n-fold X. Suppose that KX is Q-Cartier and that X is
klt near x, with zero boundary. Then

                                     vol(x,
                                     ˆ      X) ≤ 2(n − 1)n .

Equality holds if and only if
                                     (                               )
                         (X, x)an ∼
                                  = {z02 + · · · + zn2 = 0} ⊂ Cn+1 , 0 .

    The point need not be isolated in the singular locus. No structural assumption on the
singularity is implicit in Theorem 1.1. We use log discrepancy, so the discrepancy of the
exceptional divisor of the blowup of a smooth n-fold point is n. The normalized volume at
the ordinary double point is 2(n − 1)n , including its interpretation as an infimum over all
centered valuations.
    The proof uses the fourfold theorem of the companion paper The normalized-volume gap
in dimension four [44, Theorem 1.1] as its sole companion input. That theorem has the
same unrestricted boundary-zero scope and includes the analytic equality characterization;
we restate it in Section 2. The induction from this base case, developed below, proves both
the bound and the equality assertion in every higher dimension.

Corollary 1.2 (Global volume bounds). Let V be an n-dimensional K-semistable Q-Fano
variety, where n ≥ 2. If V is singular, then
                                             (        )n
                                         n n2 − 1
                                (−KV ) ≤ 2                 < 2nn .
                                             n

If V ̸∼
      = Pn , then (−KV )n ≤ 2nn , with equality precisely when V is a smooth quadric Qn ⊂ Pn+1
or P × Pn−1 . These two descriptions coincide for n = 2.
     1


    Here a Q-Fano variety is normal, projective and klt, with ample Q-Cartier anticanonical
divisor. The smaller singular bound in Corollary 1.2 is not accompanied by an assertion of
sharpness or a classification of its equality cases.

1.1   Earlier results
The gap conjecture arose from the study of singular noncollapsed polarized Kähler–Einstein
limits, where the volume density measures the size of a metric tangent cone. The algebraicity
and uniqueness of these tangent cones were established by Donaldson–Sun [10]. Spotti–Sun
proposed that the ordinary double point has the largest density among singular Ricci-flat
Kähler cones with isolated vertex, and formulated the corresponding normalized-volume
conjecture for arbitrary singular klt germs [46, Conjectures 1.2 and 5.5]. Their observation
that density above 1/2 forces Gorenstein canonical structure in the metric-limit setting [46,
Proposition 3.7] already illustrates a central feature of the problem: a sufficiently large volume
can force algebraic structure that is absent from the hypotheses. Here that principle is applied
after stable degeneration, starting from an arbitrary klt germ.
    The unrestricted low-dimensional cases precede the present induction. For surfaces,
Li–Liu’s calculation ˆ vol(0, C2 /G) = 4/|G| for finite groups acting freely in codimension
one, together with the quotient classification, gives the bound and its equality case [27,
Proposition 4.10]. Liu–Xu proved the threefold theorem for arbitrary klt germs [36, Theo-
rem 1.3]. In higher dimensions, Liu proved the conjecture for local complete intersections
[34, Theorem 1.3]. For singular Q-Gorenstein toric germs, Moraga–Süß proved the different


                                                 3
sharp bound vol  ˆ ≤ (16/27)nn for n ≥ 3, with equality precisely for the product of a three-
dimensional ordinary double point and Cn−3 ; in dimension two the bound is 2, with equality
at the surface ordinary double point [41, Theorem 2]. The fourfold companion supplies the
remaining base case used here; the higher-dimensional argument does not assume either a
complete-intersection or a toric structure.
     The global application combines the local gap with a complementary smooth theorem.
Li–Miao proved the bound 2nn and its equality classification for K-semistable Fano manifolds
other than projective space [28, Theorem 1.1]. Li–Miao–Zhang established the corresponding
metric gap for compact Kähler manifolds other than projective space with Ric(ω) ≥ (n + 1)ω,
and a global degree bound for K-semistable toric log Fano pairs whose underlying variety
is not projective space [32, Theorems 1.3 and 1.6]. The local theorem here gives a strict
improvement for singular K-semistable Q-Fano varieties, so that equality at 2nn reduces to Li–
Miao’s smooth classification. Further local refinements address the range below the threefold
maximum: Liu proves the bound 9 for Gorenstein canonical non-hypersurface threefolds and
classifies all klt threefold germs with normalized volume at least 9 [35, Theorems 1.1 and 1.2].
     The passage from metric cones to arbitrary klt singularities rests on the variational theory
of normalized volume. Martelli–Sparks–Yau proved volume minimization among Reeb fields
with fixed canonical weight [39]; Li–Liu and Li–Xu related cone metrics and K-stability to
minimization over all centered valuations [27, Theorem 1.9][29, Theorem 1.3]. For general
klt germs, existence of a minimizer, its quasi-monomiality, uniqueness up to scaling, and
finite generation were established by Blum, Xu, and Xu–Zhuang [4, 50, 51, 52]. These results
produce a K-semistable cone whose Reeb valuation computes the original normalized volume.
The further degeneration of Li–Wang–Xu gives a K-polystable cone with the same value [31,
Theorem 1.2]. Thus the cone reduction preserves the infimum over all valuations, which is
essential for a gap theorem about arbitrary germs.
     We also use lower semicontinuity [5] and the finite degree formula [51] to derive smoothness
of the puncture and Gorenstein structure from the density threshold. The new argument
begins after that reduction: it must control integral gradings approximating the minimizing
Reeb vector of an isolated Gorenstein cone, whose quotient is usually an orbifold. Passing to
the coarse quotient too early loses the cyclic characters that control both rational curves and
the eventual volume estimate.
     Several classical methods enter at this point, in different roles. The use of rational curves
belongs to the bend-and-break approach initiated by Mori [42], with stack-theoretic extensions
such as Chen–Tseng [6]. The particular curve needed here has at most one stack point and
comes from Li–Zhou [30]. Properness of twisted stable maps [1] turns its minimal degree
into a finite evaluation map. The Ricci-flat cone metric supplied by Collins–Székelyhidi [8]
then bounds the weights of symmetric tensors obtained from this map. This is related in
method to Reeb-weight obstructions for holomorphic functions [13], but the symmetric-tensor
estimate is proved here. The final high-index classification is the projective-space and quadric
characterization of Kobayashi–Ochiai [22]; the needed ample-line-bundle formulation also
follows from Araujo–Druel–Kovács [2].
     The other case uses an adjoint construction. Howald’s multiplier-ideal formula [17]
and Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing [12] lift a prescribed leading Taylor monomial after
the canonical shift. Hochster’s theorem and Stanley’s canonical-module formula [16, 47]
subsequently convert the resulting normal semigroup into a Gorenstein degeneration. None
of those statements alone forces the canonical point to be interior: that separate numerical
assertion is the content of the exponential estimate in Section 4. Its semigroup counting
follows the convex-geometric approach to graded linear series developed by Khovanskii,
Okounkov, Lazarsfeld–Mustaţă, and Kaveh–Khovanskii [21, 43, 25, 19]. The new exact
saturation conclusion is stronger than the asymptotic count supplied by that method and


                                                4
requires the adjoint argument.

1.2   The argument and its additional statements
Put n = N + 1 and
                                       )n
                                n−1                             vol(x, X)
                                 (                              ˆ
                         pn = 2             ,       d(x, X) =             .
                                 n                                 nn
Starting from the known cases in dimensions two and three and the fourfold companion,
we argue by induction. In the step n ≥ 5, for a singular germ with d(x, X) ≥ pn , stable
degeneration preserves this density and bounds the original embedding dimension by that of
a K-polystable cone C. The lower-dimensional gap and the finite degree formula force C to
be smooth off its vertex and Gorenstein. These are conclusions of the reduction, rather than
assumptions on the germ.
    A Reeb vector is a real torus grading positive on every nonconstant homogeneous function.
Approximate the minimizing Reeb ray of C by primitive integral gradings. For one such
grading, let r be the weight of a generating canonical form and let mmax be the largest
stabilizer order on the puncture. The quotient by the grading action is a smooth orbifold B,
with faithful ample weight-one line bundle L and −KB = rL. The comparison of mmax with
r/N separates the two parts of the argument.
    When mmax ≤ r/N , a minimal orbifold rational curve constrains the tangent characters.
Unless those constraints already force the grading to be free, its deformations give a finite
evaluation map onto C. Taking the product of their infinitesimal translations over the generic
sheets produces a nonzero symmetric tensor. A weight bound from the Ricci-flat cone metric
then forces a free grading with canonical weight N or N + 1. The high-index classification
identifies (B, L) as a quadric or projective space with its standard polarization, so C is an
ODP or is smooth.
    For mmax ≥ r/N , choose a point with maximal stabilizer and record each section’s
degree and leading transverse Taylor exponent. These pairs form a semigroup Γ in the
lattice determined by the stabilizer characters; write K for its closed convex cone. The
canonical form determines the lattice point c0 = (r, 1, . . . , 1). Two independent arguments
give exact control of Γ. Near-minimality of the Reeb grading gives moment inequalities, and
an exponential expectation bound puts c0 in int K. Adjoint vanishing lifts Taylor monomials
whose indices, after the shift by c0 , lie in that interior. Together these facts force rational
polyhedrality and exact saturation of Γ.
    Two filtrations convert this semigroup structure into a singular klt slice Y of the same
dimension n. A nontrivial stabilizer of order h ≥ 2 for the second filtration action makes
one character account for only 1/h of the leading valuation colength on Y . This improves
the volume comparison with C. The action and its order h are different from those defining
mmax ; the quadratic-cone example in Section 6 makes the distinction explicit.
    To use this same-dimensional slice without assuming the desired bound for it, let Mn be
the supremum of densities of singular boundary-zero klt n-fold germs. The comparison gives
                                                 pn + Mn
                                     d(o, C) ≤           .
                                                    2
Applying this estimate to densities approaching Mn proves Mn ≤ pn . The approximation
of gradings is made separately on each fixed cone; the supremum need not be attained.
In the equality case, a strict colength count and integral rounding return the cone to the
small-stabilizer case. Its ODP embedding dimension then makes the original singular germ a
hypersurface, and a weighted test forces a nondegenerate quadratic part. Figure 1 records
this case split and the return in equality.


                                                5
                     n ≥ 5, d(x, X) ≥ pn : stable degeneration and induction

                    or finite evaluation                   Adjoint lifting and saturation
                    and tensor estimate

                 Smooth projective quotient                    a singular slice Y

Figure 1: The induction step n = N + 1 ≥ 5 for a singular germ of density at least pn . Here K
is the cone of leading Taylor indices and c0 its canonical lattice point. The same-dimensional
slice enters only through the supremum Mn of singular n-dimensional densities. Equality in
the volume estimate returns the cone to the small stabilizer case.

Organization. Section 2 fixes the valuation conventions, supplies the cone reduction, and
proves the absolute grading approximation. Section 3 treats small stabilizers. For the other
case, Section 4 proves canonical interiority and Section 5 independently establishes adjoint
lifting before combining the two results. Section 6 constructs the two filtrations and the second
stabilizer. Section 7 constructs the same-dimensional singular slice, proves the supremum
inequality, and analyzes equality. Finally, Section 8 returns to the original germ and derives
the Fano consequences.


2     Normalized volume and the cone reduction
2.1   Conventions and public inputs
All varieties and stacks in the proof are over C. Boundaries are zero unless a boundary is
explicitly introduced in a vanishing argument. For a klt germ x ∈ X, write R = OX,x and
m = mx . If E is a prime divisor on a smooth proper birational model µ : X ′ → X, its log
discrepancy is
                             AX (E) = 1 + coeff E (KX ′ − µ∗ KX ).
For a real valuation v of K(X), trivial on C and centered exactly at x, put

                                                                   n! length(R/at (v))
              at (v) = {f ∈ R : v(f ) ≥ t},        vol(v) = lim                        .
                                                             t→∞           tn
The ideals are m-primary. The limit exists by [9, Theorem 5.8]: the local rings here are
analytically unramified and equicharacteristic with perfect residue field. The integer-cutoff
ideals form a graded family, and monotonicity extends the integer limit to real cutoffs.


                                                   6
    We use the standard extension of log discrepancy to real valuations. On a smooth
birational log model it is linear on each monomial cone; for an arbitrary valuation it is the
supremum over its monomial retractions [18, Proposition 5.1 and Corollary 5.4]. For the
singular Q-Gorenstein base one includes the relative canonical correction on a resolution, as
in [26, Section 2.1]. Define
                                       {
                                           AX (v)n vol(v), AX (v) < +∞,
                         vol
                         ˆ X (v) =
                                           +∞,             AX (v) = +∞.

Thus the definition never requires multiplying infinity by zero. Our normalization is

                                                                           vol(x,
                                                                           ˆ      X)
                      vol(x, X) = inf vol
                      ˆ               ˆ X (v),                 d(x, X) =             .      (2.1)
                                     v                                        nn
The infimum is unchanged if restricted to positive multiples of divisorial valuations [29,
Theorem 2.5]. Rescaling a valuation does not change its normalized volume.
   We use the following established facts in their boundary-zero form.
  (i) A klt germ has a minimizing valuation, unique up to positive scaling. It has finite
      discrepancy, is quasi-monomial, and has finitely generated associated graded. The
      latter is a K-semistable Fano cone, which admits a special equivariant degeneration
      to a K-polystable Fano cone. The minimizing Reeb vector and normalized volume
      are preserved [52, Theorem 1.2], [31, Theorem 1.2]. Uniqueness also implies that a
      minimizer normalized by discrepancy is invariant under every automorphism of the
      germ [51, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2].
 (ii) Normalized volume is lower semicontinuous in Q-Gorenstein flat families of klt germs
      with section over a normal base [5, Theorem 1]. In particular it is lower semicontinuous
      when the point moves along a curve in a fixed klt variety [5, Theorem 33(1)]. One has
      d(x, X) ≤ 1, with equality exactly at smooth points [36, Theorem 1.6].
 (iii) For a finite Galois morphism of klt germs f : (Y, y) → (X, x), with f −1 (x) = {y}
       set-theoretically and KY = f ∗ KX , the finite degree formula is

                                       vol(y,
                                       ˆ      Y ) = deg(f )vol(x,
                                                           ˆ      X).                       (2.2)

      We use this only for a quotient by a group without reflections and for the cyclic canonical
      index cover [51, Theorem 1.3].
 (iv) Isomorphic completed local rings have the same normalized volume [34, Lemma 2.15].
      Thus étale germs at complex closed points have the same invariant.
These facts concern arbitrary klt germs. In particular, the first item does not require a
divisorial minimizer, isolatedness, or smoothability.

2.2   Products and embedding dimension
Lemma 2.1 (A smooth factor). Let y ∈ Y be an N -dimensional klt germ, where N ≥ 1.
Then
                          d((y, 0), Y × A1 ) ≤ d(y, Y ).
Proof. Take a divisorial test v centered at y, of discrepancy A > 0 and volume σ, and let
a = A/N . The Gauss extension to the added parameter t is
                                       (               )
                                        ∑
                                                   i
                             (v ⊕ a)            fi t       = min{v(fi ) + ia}.
                                                               i
                                            i


                                                           7
On a log resolution this is a monomial valuation along the divisor of v and t = 0, so its log
discrepancy is A + a. Completion does not change the finite colengths. In the power-series
ring the quotient decomposes by powers of t, giving
                          (                 )        ∑              (               )
                   length R[[t]]/ak (v ⊕ a) =              length R/ak−ia (v) .
                                                 0≤i<k/a

The defining asymptotic for σ, followed by a Riemann sum, gives vol(v ⊕ a) = σ/a. Therefore

                                 (A + A/N )N +1 N σ   AN σ
                                                    =      .
                                  (N + 1)N +1 A       NN

Take the infimum over the divisorial tests on Y .

Lemma 2.2 (Lifting generators). Let v be a finite-discrepancy valuation of a klt germ, with
finitely generated positively graded associated graded ring grv R. Then

                                   edim(R) ≤ edim(grv R).

Proof. Choose minimal homogeneous algebra generators f¯1 , . . . , f¯e of grv R, all of positive
value, and lift them to f1 , . . . , fe ∈ m. To show that their classes span m/m2 , start with
g ∈ m. Its initial form is a homogeneous polynomial in the f¯i . Subtracting the corresponding
polynomial in the fi either annihilates the remainder or strictly increases its value. Every
positive value that occurs belongs to the semigroup generated by the positive numbers v(fi ),
so only finitely many such values lie below any fixed bound.
    The Izumi inequality for a finite-discrepancy valuation on a klt germ [26, Theorem 3.1]
gives v(g) ≤ c ordm (g), with a fixed constant c. In particular, a nonzero remainder of value
greater than c lies in m2 . The cancellation process therefore terminates modulo m2 after
finitely many steps. Every polynomial subtracted has no constant term, and modulo m2 is a
linear combination of the fi . This proves the assertion.

2.3   The minimum at the ordinary double point
Lemma 2.3 (The ODP minimum). For n ≥ 2, the ordinary double point Qn has

                                   vol(0,
                                   ˆ      Qn ) = 2(n − 1)n .

Proof. First take the exact quadratic cone

                    Qn = Spec R,        R = C[z0 , . . . , zn ]/(z02 + · · · + zn2 ),

with its ordinary grading. It is klt. For example, blowing up the vertex resolves it with
smooth exceptional quadric, whose log discrepancy is n − 1 > 0; further smooth blowups
preserve the klt condition.
     Normalize a minimizing valuation v by its discrepancy. Uniqueness makes it invariant
under all automorphisms, in particular under cone scalings and the connected orthogonal
group SO(n + 1, C). For each j ≥ 0, the degree-j piece Rj is the irreducible representation
of complex harmonic polynomials of degree j in n + 1 variables. To identify the quotient,
write Pj for homogeneous complex polynomials of degree j and Hj for the subspace killed by
∑ 2                                      ∑ 2
   i ∂zi ; set Pk = 0 for k < 0. For q =  zi , the harmonic decomposition Pj = Hj ⊕ qPj−2
identifies Rj with Hj ; see [14, Example 251 and Theorem 257]. The complex representation
is irreducible already under the compact group SO(n + 1), so an invariant subspace under
SO(n + 1, C) must be trivial or the whole space. For the classical harmonic-polynomial


                                                 8
formulation and its extensions, see also [38, Section 1]. This includes n = 2 and n = 3. The
exception for two ambient variables is outside the range under consideration.
    For each cutoff t, the subspace {f ∈ Rj : v(f ) ≥ t} is invariant, so it is either zero or all
of Rj . Every nonzero element of Rj consequently has a common value aj . If 0 ̸= f ∈ R1 ,
then f j ̸= 0, and valuation multiplicativity gives aj = ja1 . Invariance under cone scalings
separates homogeneous pieces of a cutoff: a finite Vandermonde combination of scalings
isolates each piece. Thus, for g = j gj ̸= 0,
                                   ∑


                                     v(g) = a1 min{j : gj ̸= 0}.

After localizing at the vertex the same assertion holds, since denominators nonzero at the
vertex have value zero. The minimizer is therefore proportional to the ordinary degree
valuation.
    That valuation is the order along the exceptional quadric of the vertex blowup. Hypersur-
face adjunction gives discrepancy n − 1, and its volume is the hypersurface multiplicity 2. It
follows that the infimum equals 2(n − 1)n .
    Finally, an analytic ordinary double point has the same completed local ring as this exact
cone. Completion invariance [34, Lemma 2.15] gives the same normalized volume.

2.4   The induction setup
The companion paper The normalized-volume gap in dimension four [44, Theorem 1.1] proves
the following base case. We state the entire interface because its equality assertion is part of
the theorem propagated here.

Theorem 2.4 (The fourfold gap). Let x be a singular closed point of a normal complex
algebraic fourfold X. Suppose that KX is Q-Cartier and X is klt near x, with zero boundary.
Then
                                     vol(x, X) ≤ 162.
                                     ˆ

Equality holds if and only if the complex analytic germ is
                              (                                      )
                                  {z02 + z12 + z22 + z32 + z42 = 0}, 0 .

No isolatedness, complete-intersection, quotient, or smoothability assumption is made.

   For k ≥ 2 set
                                                          )k
                                                 k−1
                                                 (
                                          pk = 2               .                            (2.3)
                                                  k
Let Mk be the supremum of d(x, X) over all singular boundary-zero klt k-fold germs: the
varieties are normal and complex algebraic, and their canonical divisors are Q-Cartier. This
supremum is finite, since Mk ≤ 1. The numbers pk are strictly increasing: for real t > 1,
                         d                                     1
                            [t log(1 − 1/t)] = log(1 − 1/t) +     > 0.
                         dt                                   t−1
The last inequality is log(1 + u) < u, with u = 1/(t − 1).
    The dimension-two case of Theorem 1.1 follows from the quotient classification of klt
surface singularities [7, Proposition 6.11]. The germ is analytically isomorphic to (A2 /G, 0),
where G is a finite effective linear group acting without reflections. Analytic isomorphism
identifies the completed local rings, so completion invariance transfers the normalized volume
to this algebraic quotient. The finite degree formula gives d = 1/|G|. If the germ is singular,
|G| ≥ 2, and equality with p2 = 1/2 forces an order-two action without a fixed hyperplane,

                                                   9
namely (−1, −1). This is the A1 surface singularity. The threefold case is [36, Theorem 1.3(1)],
and the fourfold case is Theorem 2.4.
    Henceforth, until the induction is closed, assume Theorem 1.1 in dimensions below n, and
fix
                              n = N + 1 ≥ 5,        d(x, X) ≥ pn ,                        (2.4)
with x singular. The only use of Mn will be its definition as a supremum, not an unproved
upper bound in dimension n.

Proposition 2.5 (Cone reduction). Under (2.4), there is a singular K-polystable Fano cone
C = Spec S, with vertex o, such that

                      d(o, C) = d(x, X),      edim(X, x) ≤ edim(C, o).

The puncture C \ {o} is smooth, S is a normal Gorenstein ring, and its canonical module has
a homogeneous generator. The cone has zero boundary.

Proof. Apply stable degeneration to a minimizer at x, and then take the K-polystable special
degeneration. In the first passage the induced Reeb valuation has the same volume and
discrepancy as the original minimizer [29, Lemma 4.10]. In the second, equivariant flatness
preserves the dimensions of the character spaces and hence the Reeb volume. The relative
canonical character is constant, so its discrepancy is also preserved. Li–Xu’s characterization
of K-semistability [29, Theorem 1.3] shows that the final Reeb valuation minimizes normalized
volume over all centered valuations. Thus the two passages preserve the infimum in (2.1),
not only the number of an arbitrary test.
    Lemma 2.2 gives the embedding-dimension inequality for the first passage. Upper semi-
continuity along the vertex section of the special flat degeneration gives it for the second.
The final vertex is therefore singular.
    Choose any positive integral grading of S, and let P ̸= o. Its grading orbit specializes to
o, so lower semicontinuity gives
                                       d(o, C) ≤ d(P, C).                                 (2.5)
Choose a homogeneous function f , of degree d > 0, with c = f (P ) ̸= 0, and put YP = {f =
c} ⊂ Cf . The action map

                           YP × Gm −→ Cf ,         (Q, a) 7−→ a · Q,

is the finite étale cover obtained by adjoining a root ad = f /c. Near (P, 1), it expresses the
germ as the product of the N -dimensional slice (YP , P ) and a smooth curve. The slice is
klt by this étale description. If P were singular, the slice would be singular as well. The
induction hypothesis, Lemma 2.1, and étale invariance would then imply

                                d(P, C) ≤ pN < pn ≤ d(o, C),

contrary to (2.5). Thus the puncture is smooth.
    Let q be the canonical index at o. The cyclic index cover has degree q, is quasi-étale
and crepant, and is klt. It has one point over o. Indeed, its algebra is the direct sum of the
reflexive canonical powers modulo q. If a homogeneous element of a nonzero residue degree
were not nilpotent in the fiber over o, a power returning to degree zero would be a unit.
The corresponding section would trivialize a proper positive canonical power, contradicting
minimality of q. Thus the nonzero residue-degree pieces are nilpotent, and the reduced fiber
consists of one point. Equation (2.2) and the upper bound d ≤ 1 give d(o, C) ≤ 1/q. Since
pn > 1/2, necessarily q = 1.


                                              10
    Klt singularities are Cohen–Macaulay [24, Definition 117 and Theorem 120]. The canonical
module ωS is invertible at the vertex, and a homogeneous element generating its one-
dimensional fiber there generates it after localization. Its graded cokernel has empty support:
any nonempty closed support invariant under a positive grading contains the vertex. Since ωS
is torsion-free, the resulting map S → ωS is injective as well. It is therefore an isomorphism,
with a grading shift.

2.5   Integral gradings and orbifold quotients
Fix the cone of Proposition 2.5. Let T be an effective algebraic torus of automorphisms
containing its Reeb vector ξ, and normalize

                                             A(ξ) = n.

Choose a T-eigen-generator ΩC of ωS . Its character pairs with cocharacters as the linear
discrepancy functional A [29, Lemmas 2.16 and 2.18]. Function weights use the convention
g(aP ) = aj g(P ); the differential dg has the same weight. The Reeb cone consists of
cocharacters positive on all nonconstant homogeneous functions.

Lemma 2.6 (Fast primitive approximations). There are primitive positive integral cocharac-
ters ζi , of canonical weights ri = A(ζi ) ∈ Z>0 , such that
                                         ri
                                  ζi =      ξ + ϵi ,     ϵi −→ 0                            (2.6)
                                         n
in the real cocharacter space. If the ray of ξ is rational, the sequence may be chosen constant
and exact. Otherwise ri → ∞.
    The normalized volumes of the degree valuations wtζi tend to ˆ      vol(o, C). For any fixed
finite set of homogeneous algebra generators, their ζi -degrees lie between cri and Cri for
positive constants c, C. Consequently the largest stabilizer order mmax,i on the puncture is
O(ri ).

Proof. In the quotient of real cocharacter space by its integral lattice, recurrence gives ti → ∞
and integral cocharacters qi with qi = ti ξ + ei , where ei → 0. One may obtain such a sequence
from simultaneous Dirichlet approximation, or from returns to zero of the one-parameter
subgroup in its compact closure. Let di be the gcd of qi in a lattice basis and put ζi = qi /di .
Then
                                 A(ζi )      1          A(ei )
                                                (               )
                            ζi −        ξ=         ei −        ξ −→ 0.
                                   n         di          n
The cocharacters are positive for large i. If their positive integers ri = A(ζi ) had a bounded
subsequence, (2.6) would make ζi bounded on that subsequence. A constant lattice sub-
sequence would then give ζ = (r/n)ξ, forcing the ray to be rational. The rational case is
handled by its primitive generator.
    Choose homogeneous algebra generators g1 , . . . , ga with T-characters χ1 , . . . , χa . Each
⟨χj , ξ⟩ is positive, so (2.6) gives the asserted two-sided bounds for their integral degrees.
More precisely, the normalized cocharacters (n/ri )ζi converge to ξ. Uniform comparison on
the finite set of generator characters then compares their values on every occurring character:
each is a sum of generator characters with nonnegative integer coefficients. It follows that the
valuation ideals of the normalized degree valuations are squeezed between those of wtξ with
cutoff factors tending to one. Their volumes therefore converge; their discrepancies are all n.
    At a nonvertex point some generator is nonzero. Its stabilizer for a primitive grading is
cyclic, and its order divides the degree of every nonvanishing generator. It is therefore at
most the largest generator degree, proving the final assertion.

                                                  11
   In what follows, sufficiently fast gradings always means gradings in a sequence as in
Lemma 2.6, including the exact constant sequence on a rational ray. All constants may
depend on the fixed cone. No uniformity over the class defining Mn is asserted or needed.

Lemma 2.7 (The quotient orbifold). For a primitive positive integral grading ζ, of canonical
weight r, let
                                 B = [(C \ {o})/Gm ].
Then B is a smooth effective proper orbifold of dimension N , with projective coarse space
Proj S. It has a faithful ample weight-one line bundle L such that

                               Sj = H 0 (B, jL),     −KB = rL.                              (2.7)

Every stabilizer is a finite cyclic group. At a point of order m, a smooth transverse uniformizer
carries a faithful µm -action, and L has a faithful fiber character.

Proof. The smooth puncture has finite stabilizers for the positive grading, so its quotient
stack is smooth and Deligne–Mumford. It is the usual stack associated with a positively
graded affine ring away from its vertex; its coarse space is Proj S, and a sufficiently divisible
positive power of the weight-one line descends to an ample coarse line bundle. This also
proves properness.
    The grading is effective because the integral cocharacter is primitive in an effective torus.
At a point, the finite stabilizer acts trivially on the tangent line of the orbit. If an element
acted trivially also on a transverse tangent space, it would have identity differential on the
smooth puncture. A finite-order automorphism in characteristic zero is formally linearizable
at a fixed point; hence that element would be the identity on a neighborhood and thus on
the irreducible cone, contrary to effectiveness. This proves faithfulness of the transverse
representation and effectiveness of the orbifold. The weight-one character of the subgroup of
Gm is faithful by construction.
    Sections of jL are the homogeneous functions of degree j on the puncture. Normality and
the codimension of the vertex extend them to C, giving the first equality in (2.7). Contracting
ΩC with the Euler field gives a horizontal top form of character r, so KB = −rL.

   We retain the stack B, its faithful line L, and the character information throughout the
argument. In particular, we do not replace L by a coarse line bundle before the stabilizers
have been shown to be trivial.


3    Small stabilizers
We use Proposition 2.5 and Lemmas 2.6 and 2.7. Thus C = Spec S is a normal Gorenstein
Fano cone of dimension n = N + 1, where N ≥ 4, its puncture C ◦ = C \ {o} is smooth,
and the polarized cone (C, ξ) is K-polystable, with minimizing Reeb vector normalized
by A(ξ) = n. Fix homogeneous torus eigenfunctions f1 , . . . , fq generating S, with torus
characters α1 , . . . , αq . For a primitive positive integral grading ζ, write

                        r = A(ζ),      B = [C ◦ /Gm ],      −KB = rL.

Here L is the faithful ample orbifold line bundle of weight one. The maximum stabilizer
order for this grading is denoted by mmax . All constants in this section may depend on the
fixed cone, its torus and the displayed generators.




                                               12
Theorem 3.1 (Small-stabilizer classification). Let ζi be primitive positive integral gradings
satisfying
                     ri                                                                 ri
              ζi =      ξ + ϵi ,       ri = A(ζi ),        ∥ϵi ∥ −→ 0,   mmax (ζi ) ≤      .   (3.1)
                     n                                                                  N
For all sufficiently large i, every stabilizer is trivial and ri ∈ {N, N + 1}. More precisely, the
polarized quotient is                    {
                                       ∼   (PN , OPN (1)), ri = N + 1,
                            (Bi , Li ) =
                                           (QN , OQN (1)), ri = N,
where QN ⊂ PN +1 is a smooth quadric. Consequently the cone C is respectively smooth or
an ordinary double point. The assertion includes the constant exact primitive grading when
the ray of ξ is rational.

    We begin with a minimal orbifold rational curve. Its tangent characters either force r = N
and trivial stabilizers, or its deformations yield a finite evaluation map and hence a nonzero
symmetric tensor of negative weight. A metric lower bound for homogeneous symmetric
tensors, together with an approximation estimate uniform in their rank, gives the remaining
rigidity.

3.1    A minimal orbifold rational curve
For the moment fix one primitive grading satisfying

                                               mmax ≤ r/N.                                     (3.2)

The orbifold B is smooth and effective, is proper with projective coarse space, and has
ample anticanonical bundle rL. We use the orbifold rational-curve theorem of Li–Zhou [30,
Proposition 2.6]. In this setting it supplies a representable nonconstant map from P(1, ℓ),
where the only possible stack point is infinity, whose anticanonical degree plus the inverse
age at that point is at most dim B + 1. In particular its anticanonical degree is at most n.
No positivity assumption on TB is required for this assertion.
    Choose a map of least positive L-degree among all representable nonconstant maps of this
form, allowing ℓ = 1. Such a minimum exists: representability embeds the source stabilizer
in a target stabilizer, so the denominators of these degrees divide one of the finitely many
integers at most mmax . Write

                           f : P(1, ℓ) −→ B,           f ∗L ∼
                                                            = O(e),      e > 0,

and let m be the stabilizer order of its value at infinity. This endpoint order need not equal
mmax . Thus ℓ | m, and minimality and the existence theorem give re/ℓ ≤ n. On the other
hand, r/m ≥ N by Equation (3.2). Hence

                                            em   re/ℓ   N +1
                                      1≤       =      ≤      < 2.                              (3.3)
                                             ℓ   r/m     N

The expression em/ℓ is an integer. We obtain

                                   e = 1,     ℓ = m,         N ≤ r/m ≤ n.                      (3.4)

  Choose an identification f ∗ L ∼
                                 = O(1). Passing to its grading torsor gives an equivariant
map
                   F : A2 \ {0} −→ C ◦ ,     F (tx, tm y) = t · F (x, y).

                                                      13
Since A2 is normal and C is affine, the coordinate functions extend uniquely across the origin.
Thus F : A2 (1, m) → C is a homogeneous polynomial map. Set P = F (0, 1); its stabilizer is
µm . Conversely, a homogeneous map with no preimage of the vertex outside the origin, and
with this degree-one torsor identification, gives a representable map to B: its maps on source
inertia groups are the inclusions inherited from the identity homomorphism of the grading
groups.

Lemma 3.2 (Deformations with a fixed lift). Let b′1 , . . . , b′n ∈ {1, . . . , m} represent the
characters of µm on TC,P , with the trivial character represented by m. Every component
through F of the scheme of homogeneous maps F ′ : A2 (1, m) → C satisfying F ′ (0, 1) = P has
dimension at least
                                             r   ∑n
                                                     b′j
                                   χ=n+        −         .                                  (3.5)
                                            m j=1 m

In particular this dimension is at least n, except possibly when r/m = N and the entire
tangent action at P is trivial.

Proof. Homogeneous maps form an affine scheme of finite type: in fixed homogeneous
generators of S, each coordinate of the map is a polynomial of a specified weighted degree,
and the relations of S give polynomial equations in their finitely many coefficients. The
condition of avoiding the vertex outside the origin is open, as may be checked on the proper
weighted line. Near the given map, deformation theory can therefore be performed entirely
in the smooth target C ◦ .
    Let E be the rank-n bundle on P(1, m) obtained by descending F ∗ TC ◦ . Its determinant is
O(r), so deg E = r/m. We are deforming an equivariant map with its source and its grading
torsor fixed; equivalently, we are deforming a section of the associated smooth bundle, with
the canonical section obstruction theory of [49, Theorem 4.13 and Equation (4.18)]. There
is no quotient by source automorphisms or by changes of the torsor identification. If D∞
denotes the residual gerbe at infinity, the tangent and obstruction spaces for fixing its value
are
                     H 0 (P(1, m), E(−D∞ )),      H 1 (P(1, m), E(−D∞ )).
Thus their Euler characteristic is a lower bound for the dimension of every component through
the map.
    For completeness, orbifold Riemann–Roch here says χ(E) = n + deg E − age(E∞ ). It
follows by taking the coarse pushforward: locally diagonalizing at the stack point subtracts
the fractional character weights from the degree, after which ordinary Riemann–Roch on P1
applies. Restriction to D∞ has Euler characteristic equal to the dimension of the invariant
fiber, because µm is linearly reductive. Subtracting that invariant dimension is precisely the
effect of representing each trivial character by m instead of zero. The exact sequence for
restriction to D∞ therefore gives Equation (3.5).
           ∑ ′
    Since     bj /m ≤ n, we have χ ≥ r/m. The Euler characteristic χ is an integer. If
r/m > N , it is at least N + 1 = n. If r/m = N and some character is nontrivial, the
inequality is strict and the same conclusion follows.




                                               14
3.2    Finite evaluation and its symmetric tensor
Assume that the exception in Lemma 3.2 does not occur. Let H be the reduced closure of an
irreducible component of the open locus of maps avoiding the vertex outside the origin, in
the affine scheme of homogeneous maps with F ′ (0, 1) = P . Then H is integral and
                                            dim H ≥ n.                                         (3.6)
Precomposition with (x, y) 7→ (ax, y) preserves the chosen component because the acting
group Gm is connected. It gives a positive grading on H: every coefficient involving x has
positive weight, whereas the coefficients involving only y are fixed by P . All maps contract to
the same map obtained by deleting the terms involving x. Consider the equivariant evaluation
morphism
                              ev : H −→ C,        F ′ 7−→ F ′ (1, 0).                      (3.7)
Lemma 3.3 (Finite evaluation). The morphism in Equation (3.7) is finite and surjective.
Its fiber over o is supported at the unique contracted map.
Proof. Take F0 ∈ H with F0 (1, 0) = o. Choose a pointed curve in H through F0 , with general
point in the locus avoiding the vertex, and normalize it. Its generic map gives a twisted
stable graph map to B × P1 : the second map is the coarse identification of P(1, m) with P1 ,
and infinity is marked. This graph is stable even before any contraction because its second
map has degree one. After a finite base change, properness of twisted stable maps gives a
limiting graph map [1, Theorem 4.3]. The target is a tame proper smooth Deligne–Mumford
stack with projective coarse space, as required by that theorem.
    There is a unique component of the limiting coarse source of second degree one. It maps
isomorphically to P1 ; call it the horizontal component. All other components form rational
trees attached to it, since the total arithmetic genus is zero. The first map on the horizontal
component is the coarse rational map defined by F0 , after cancellation of its basepoints.
Indeed the two maps agree on the open set where the limiting homogeneous coordinates do
not vanish simultaneously.
    We spell out why a positive-degree tail occurs over the finite basepoint [1 : 0]. Choose a
sufficiently divisible integer k such that kL descends to a very ample bundle on the coarse
space of B, and m | k. Its pullback along the original maps is the coarse bundle OP1 (k/m).
The limiting projective coordinates are binary forms of that degree. They have a common zero
at [1 : 0], because F0 (1, 0) = o, and are not all zero, because F0 (0, 1) = P ̸= o. Cancelling their
common divisor loses positive degree at [1 : 0]. A general hyperplane avoiding the value of the
canceled map at that point has the lost positive number of inverse-image points specializing
there. In the limiting stable map these points cannot lie on the horizontal component. They
are therefore accounted for by positive first degree on a tree over [1 : 0]. This also proves the
degree assertion directly, without making an assumption about components that might occur
over infinity.
    Choose a terminal leaf of that tree. It does not contain the infinity marking, since its
second image is [1 : 0]. It has one node and no markings. If its first map had degree zero, it
would be constant in both factors and unstable: stability requires the induced coarse map to
be a Kontsevich stable map [1, Section 4], and an unmarked constant terminal leaf has only
one special point. Hence its first degree is positive. Its normalization is a twisted rational
curve with at most one stack point: the only allowed stack points of a twisted source are
nodes and markings. Projection from the product target to B preserves representability,
since P1 has trivial inertia. The leaf consequently gives a representable nonconstant map
P(1, ℓ′ ) → B of the type used in the minimum.
    Its L-degree is at least the original minimal degree 1/m. Degree is additive on the limiting
source and every component has nonnegative L-degree, while the total degree is 1/m. Thus

                                                 15
this leaf consumes the full first degree. The horizontal component has first degree zero, and
its constant value is the coarse image of P . It follows that the image of the affine map F0 lies
in the closure of the grading orbit of P .
    The normalization of that orbit closure is A1 , with a parameter of grading weight m,
normalized to have value one at P . To see the weight, the gcd of the degrees of the coordinates
nonzero at P is its stabilizer order m. The map from the normal source A2 factors through
this normalization: its parameter is integral over the coordinate ring of the orbit curve
and hence regular on A2 . The parameter pulled back along F0 is a weighted homogeneous
polynomial of degree m, so it has the form

                                             y + cxm .

The coefficient of y is one because the value at (0, 1) is fixed. Evaluation at (1, 0) is the vertex
only if c = 0. Therefore the vertex fiber is supported at the single contracted map.
    Finally, let RH be the positively graded coordinate ring of H. The preceding fiber
statement says that RH /S+ RH is finite dimensional. Lift a homogeneous basis of this
quotient. Induction on the positive degree shows that these lifts generate RH as an S-module;
this is graded Nakayama. Thus evaluation is finite. Its image is closed and has dimension
dim H ≥ n, by Equation (3.6). Since C is integral of dimension n, the image is all of C, and
dim H = n.

Lemma 3.4 (A tensor of negative integral weight). Let b be the degree of the finite evaluation
in Lemma 3.3. There is a nonzero algebraic section

                                     s ∈ H 0 (C ◦ , Symb TC ◦ )

of integral-grading weight −bm.

Proof. The source automorphisms (x, y) 7→ (x, y + txm ), for t ∈ C, preserve the homogeneous-
map scheme, the fixed value at (0, 1), and its open locus avoiding the vertex. The connected
additive group therefore preserves the component H. Its vector field is nonzero: a coordinate
nonzero at P has a nonzero pure power of y, whose derivative under this action is nonzero in
characteristic zero. Differentiating evaluation gives a regular vector V along evaluation over
C ◦ . It is generically nonzero, since the finite dominant evaluation is generically separable
and hence has injective differential on a nonempty smooth open set. For a target coordinate
of degree d, its component is ∂y F ′ (1, 0), of coefficient-grading degree d − m. Thus V , as a
vector along evaluation, has derivation weight −m.
     Over the generic point, take the symmetric product of the vectors on all b sheets. This
gives a nonzero element of Symb TC ◦ over C(C); the product, unlike the ordinary trace, cannot
cancel. It is invariant under permutation of the sheets and so descends to that field. It
is regular as well. On a smooth affine open set of C ◦ trivializing the tangent bundle, the
components of V lie in a finite algebra over the base ring. The coefficients of their symmetric
product are therefore integral over the base ring and lie in its fraction field. Normality of the
base makes them regular. This argument does not require H to be normal; alternatively one
can first use its finite normalization. The construction is equivariant and multiplies weights
by b, giving weight −bm.




                                                16
3.3   A bound for homogeneous symmetric tensors
The tensor just constructed has negative weight for the integral grading. To exploit this,
we first bound the Reeb weight of a homogeneous symmetric tensor. By the Fano cone
Yau–Tian–Donaldson theorem [8, Theorem 1.1 and Definitions 2.1–2.2], C ◦ carries a Ricci-flat
Kähler cone metric with Reeb vector ξ. The theorem applies here because the puncture
is smooth and the singularity is Q-Gorenstein and klt. The condition called K-stability in
that reference allows equality only for an isomorphic central fiber, and is the K-polystability
condition used here. With A(ξ) = n, the real homothetic dilations have infinitesimal generator
−Jξ, and their pullback multiplies the metric by the square of the dilation factor.
Lemma 3.5 (Tensor weight bound). Let b ≥ 1, and let s be a nonzero homogeneous algebraic
section of Symb TC ◦ , of ξ-weight τ , with vector fields weighted as derivations. Then

                                             τ ≥ −b.

Proof. The Chern connection induced on Symb TC ◦ has zero mean curvature: contraction of
the curvature on TC ◦ is Ricci curvature, and contraction commutes with the induced tensor
and symmetric power operations. Put u = |s|2 . The holomorphic Bochner formula and
Cauchy–Schwarz give, with a consistent positive complex-Laplacian normalization,

                            ∆u = |∇1,0 s|2 ≥ 0,        |∂u|2 ≤ u ∆u.

Consequently log(u + a) is subharmonic for each a > 0, and so is (u + a)p/2 for every p > 0,
by the chain rule applied to the increasing convex exponential function. Letting a decrease
to zero shows that |s|p is subharmonic in the distributional sense, including across the zero
set of s.
    Let ρ be the metric radial coordinate and M = {ρ = 1} its compact smooth link. A
contravariant tensor of rank b and derivation weight τ has norm of radial degree τ + b. If
τ + b < 0, choose p > 0 such that

                                 d = p(τ + b) ∈ (2 − 2n, 0).

Then |s|p = ρd ϕ for a nonnegative continuous function ϕ on M with positive integral. The
cone-Laplacian formula, valid also distributionally, is

                          ∆(ρd ϕ) = ρd−2 d(d + 2n − 2)ϕ + ∆M ϕ .
                                         (                         )


Integrating the angular term over M gives zero. Testing subharmonicity against
                                                                            ∫
                                                                               a nonnegative
radial function supported in an annulus would therefore imply d(d + 2n − 2) M ϕ ≥ 0, which
is impossible. Thus τ + b ≥ 0.

3.4   Uniform control of characters and the conclusion
The tensor rank in Lemma 3.4 can vary with the grading. The following estimate makes the
approximation error independent of that rank.
Lemma 3.6 (Character estimate). There is a constant c > 0 with the following property
for all sufficiently close gradings in Equation (3.1). If a nonzero rank-b tensor on C ◦ has
integral-grading weight −bm, with m > 0, then it has a nonzero torus eigencomponent of
character χ satisfying
                                          ∥χ∥ ≤ cb.
Consequently, if the tensor is as in Lemma 3.4, then
                                              r
                                       m≤       + c∥ϵ∥.                                   (3.8)
                                              n

                                               17
Proof. For the fixed eigen-generators fj , positivity of ξ and absolute convergence of the error
give constants c1 , c2 > 0 such that their integral degrees dj = αj (ζ) satisfy

                                 c1 r ≤ dj ≤ c2 r   for every j.                           (3.9)

These bounds include the exact rational grading.
    The differentials dfj span the cotangent bundle of C ◦ . Pairing a symmetric tensor with
all ordered b-tuples of these differentials embeds its space of sections into a finite tuple of
regular functions on C ◦ . Normality extends these functions over o. This also shows that the
torus action on sections is locally finite, so the tensor has a nonzero torus eigencomponent;
every such component retains its specified ζ-weight.
    Let χ be the character of a nonzero component, and choose a nonzero pairing with
dfj1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ dfjb . Its function has character β = χ + αj1 + · · · + αjb and integral degree

                            0 ≤ d = −bm + dj1 + · · · + djb ≤ c2 rb.

It has a polynomial lift in the generators consisting of monomials of character β, by torus
equivariance of the polynomial presentation of S. Each such monomial contains at most
d/(c1 r) ≤ (c2 /c1 )b factors, by Equation (3.9). As the generator characters are fixed, this
proves ∥β∥ = O(b), and then ∥χ∥ = O(b), uniformly in the tensor, its rank and the grading.
    Put τ = χ(ξ). The eigencomponent satisfies Lemma 3.5, so τ ≥ −b. On the other hand,
                                          r             r

                                          n             n
Dividing by b proves Equation (3.8).

Proof of Theorem 3.1. For each grading choose the minimal curve and its stabilizer order m
as above. If the exceptional case in Lemma 3.2 occurs, then r/m = N and the µm -action
on TC,P is trivial. Faithfulness of the transverse tangent action implies m = 1, hence r = N .
Equation (3.2) then forces mmax = 1.
    For the remaining indices, Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4 apply. The character estimate and
Equation (3.4) give
                                      0 ≤ nm − r ≤ nc∥ϵ∥.
The left side is an integer. Since the error tends to zero, we have nm = r for all sufficiently
large indices. For a rational ray with its constant exact grading the error is zero, so this
equality holds directly.
    Now the finite evaluation has dim H = n, whereas its deformation dimension satisfies

                                         r   n

                                                           n

                                         m j=1 m          j=1
                                                              m

All equalities must hold. In particular every b′j = m, so the tangent action is trivial. Its
faithfulness again gives m = 1, and now r = n = N + 1. Finally
                                               N +1

                                                N
forces mmax = 1.
    The quotient is therefore an ordinary smooth projective Fano N -fold and L an actual
ample line bundle. The Kobayashi–Ochiai theorem in its ample-line-bundle formulation [22],
also supplied by [2, Theorems 1.1 and 1.3], applied to −KB = rL with r = N + 1 or N , gives
precisely the two polarized varieties stated in the theorem. The polarization is the standard

one, as also follows by substituting into their Picard groups. By the section-ring identity

This is the polynomial ring for (PN , O(1)), and the homogeneous coordinate ring of a

or the n-dimensional ordinary double point.


4     Jet cones and the canonical interior point
We work with the fixed cone supplied by Proposition 2.5. Thus C = Spec S has dimension
n = N + 1, its puncture is smooth, and its canonical module has a homogeneous nowhere-
vanishing generator on the puncture. The minimizing Reeb vector ξ is normalized by
AC (ξ) = n. Throughout this section,

                                         vol(o,
                                         ˆ      C) ≥ 2N n .                                   (4.1)

Take the primitive positive gradings of Lemma 2.6, so that

                       ζν = (rν /n)ξ + ϵν ,         rν = AC (ζν ),          ϵν −→ 0

in absolute cocharacter norm. In the rational case we use the exact constant grading. Consider
a subsequence on which the largest stabilizer order satisfies mν ≥ rν /N , and choose a point
attaining that order. We suppress the index ν when discussing a single grading. Constants
carrying a subscript C may depend on this fixed cone and on N ; no uniformity over different
cones is needed.

4.1    Leading Taylor terms and the real cone
Let B and L be the smooth quotient orbifold and its weight-one line bundle from Lemma 2.7.
In particular,
                           Sj = H 0 (B, jL),      −KB = rL.
At the chosen point, take a smooth equivariant uniformizer with parameters z1 , . . . , zN
and stabilizer µm . Choose the parameters and the frame of L so that their characters are
respectively b1 , . . . , bN ∈ Z/m and 1. We choose these algebraically: averaging regular lifts of
a cotangent eigenbasis gives an equivariant map to AN that is étale at the chosen point, and
averaging a nonvanishing local frame gives the specified line character. After shrinking, these
are equivariant algebraic étale coordinates and an algebraic frame. A section of jL is then
represented by a power series F (z) satisfying

                                 F (εb1 z1 , . . . , εbN zN ) = εj F (z).

Order monomials first by total degree and then lexicographically, with the smallest monomial
first. Write in(s) = z γ for the leading monomial, omitting its nonzero scalar coefficient, and
put

                        Γ = {(j, γ) : 0 ̸= s ∈ Sj , in(s) = z γ },                            (4.2)
                        Λ = {(j, γ) ∈ Z × ZN : j ≡
                                                          ∑
                                                              i bi γi   (mod m)},             (4.3)
                                                    N
                       K = cone(Γ) ⊂ R × R .                                                  (4.4)



                                                    19
Here (0, 0) ∈ Γ, and γ = 0 denotes a nonzero constant Taylor term, including those of sections
of positive degree. The degree coordinate in Equations (4.2)–(4.4) is the original degree j.
    For integrations only, introduce the scaled degree and the number
                                    r                        j   Nj
                             s=       ≤ 1,          D0 =       =    .                     (4.5)
                                   Nm                       sm   r

We distinguish the coordinate D0 from j throughout. Write K̃, Γ̃, and Λ̃ for the images of
K, Γ, and Λ under (j, x) 7→ (N j/r, x).

Proposition 4.1 (Jet setup). The following assertions hold.
  (i) Γ is an additive semigroup with one-dimensional leaves, and its generated group is
      exactly Λ. Every finite compatible Taylor jet is realized by sections of all sufficiently
      large degrees in each admissible progression.
 (ii) K is a full-dimensional closed convex cone, contains the positive constant ray, projects
      onto the whole exponent orthant, and satisfies K = int K. Its bounded-degree sections
      are bounded. More precisely, uniformly in the chosen point and nearby grading,
                                         ∑              j
                                |γ| :=       γi ≤ CC          ((j, γ) ∈ K).               (4.6)
                                         i
                                                        r

     Its scaled image has the form

                                K̃ = {(D0 , x) : x ∈ RN
                                                      ≥0 , D0 ≥ f (x)},                   (4.7)

     where f is finite, positively homogeneous, convex, and

                                      f (x) ≥ cC |x|        (x ∈ RN
                                                                  ≥0 )                    (4.8)

      for a constant cC > 0 independent of the nearby grading and chosen point.
 (iii) In the scaled coordinates the lattice density is s. If ℓ is a linear functional strictly
       positive on K̃ \ {0}, then

                       #{γ ′ ∈ Γ̃ : ℓ(γ ′ ) < q}
                                                                                          (4.9)
                             = s Leb{(D0 , x) ∈ K̃ : ℓ(D0 , x) < 1} q n + o(q n ),

     with Lebesgue measure in the scaled coordinates. No saturation assumption on Γ is
     required.
 (iv) The vector
                          c0 = (r, 1)        in the original (j, γ) coordinates          (4.10)
     belongs to Λ. Its scaled coordinates are (N, 1).

Proof. Leading monomials multiply, and the associated leading coefficient is a scalar. This
proves additivity and the one-dimensional-leaf assertion. In particular, each leading index in
a fixed degree accounts for one dimension of Sj .
    Choose an integer M > 0 divisible by all stabilizer orders such that M L descends to
an ample line bundle on the coarse space. In a fixed residue class j0 modulo M , prescribe
a finite compatible Taylor jet of a section of j0 L. The kernel of the map to that finite jet
space is coherent. Serre vanishing after tensoring by sufficiently large powers of M L, or
after exact tame pushdown to the coarse space, makes the map on global sections surjective.
Thus the prescribed jet is realized in every sufficiently large degree j0 + kM . Taking all the

                                                   20
finitely many admissible residue classes proves the assertion about progressions. In particular,
constants occur in all sufficiently large degrees divisible by m, and each monomial z γ occurs
as a leading term in sufficiently large compatible degrees.
      Differences of two such constant indices whose degrees differ by m give (m, 0) in the
generated group. For each i, a realized linear jet gives an index (ji , ei ) with ji ≡ bi (mod m).
The vectors (m, 0), (j1 , e1 ), . . . , (jN , eN ) generate the full congruence lattice in Equation (4.3).
All indices satisfy that congruence, proving equality of groups. These same indices show
that the cone contains the positive constant ray, has full dimension, and projects onto the
exponent orthant.
      We next prove the uniform estimate. Fix torus eigen-generators of S and the resulting
affine embedding of C. Their ζν -degrees are bounded below by a fixed positive multiple of
rν for all sufficiently large ν, because their ξ-weights are positive. A section of degree j has
a homogeneous polynomial lift in these generators, of ordinary polynomial degree at most
Cj/r. At a smooth point of the punctured cone, a homogeneous function has the same local
vanishing order as its restriction to a transverse slice: in orbit and slice coordinates it is a
unit power of the orbit coordinate times its slice expression.
      Take a general complete-intersection curve through the smooth point, cut out by affine
hyperplanes in the fixed embedding. It is smooth there and is not contained in the zero locus
of the nonzero function. The local intersection multiplicity with the function is at least its
local vanishing order. Bézout’s inequality bounds this multiplicity by the polynomial degree
times the degree of the fixed embedded cone. This proves Equation (4.6) for Γ, and then for
K by homogeneity and closure. In particular, bounded degree cuts are compact.
      The positive constant ray makes every nonempty fiber over an exponent x an upper ray
in degree. Every exponent fiber is nonempty, since nonnegative combinations of the indices
(ji , ei ) reach every x ≥ 0. Closedness and the degree bound make the lowest degree in each
fiber attainable. Hence K is the epigraph of a finite convex positively homogeneous function
in the scaled coordinates. Equation (4.6) becomes Equation (4.8). A full-dimensional closed
convex cone is the closure of its interior.
      The original lattice has covolume m. The coordinate change (j, γ) 7→ (N j/r, γ) multi-
plies covolumes by N/r; the resulting covolume is N m/r = 1/s. For clarity, we give the
nonsaturated semigroup counting argument. This is the conductor-and-exhaustion method
for value semigroups [19, Theorems 1.4 and 1.6], also used for graded linear series in [25,
Proposition 2.1]. Its asymptotic conclusion does not assert exact saturation. Let Γ0 be a
finitely generated subsemigroup with full generated group Λ, and let K0 be its cone. There is
a vector c ∈ Γ0 such that
                                               c + (K0 ∩ Λ) ⊂ Γ0 .                                 (4.11)
Indeed every lattice point of K0 lies in a cone generated by a linearly independent subset of
the finite generating set. Removing the integer parts of its nonnegative coefficients writes it
as a semigroup element plus a lattice point in one of finitely many bounded parallelepipeds.
There are only finitely many possible remainders v. Since the group is Λ, write each such
remainder as v = v+ − v− with v± ∈ Γ0 . The sum of all the v− is a single c for which
Equation (4.11) holds. Translating a bounded linear cutoff changes its scale by a constant,
so ordinary lattice counting between c + (K0 ∩ Λ) and K0 ∩ Λ gives its leading lattice volume.
After the coordinate change this is Euclidean volume with density s.
    Now exhaust int K by cones of finitely many indices of Γ, always retaining a fixed finite
set whose group is Λ. Every interior point belongs to the interior of one of these finite cones:
choose a small simplex surrounding it in int K and approximate the simplex vertices by
elements of cone(Γ). The resulting finite cones give the lower leading count. Counting all
lattice points of K gives the upper count. Compact convex cutoff bodies have boundary
of Lebesgue measure zero, and their volumes are exhausted from the interior. This proves

                                                   21
Equation (4.9).
   Finally, on the uniformizer the canonical character is the negative of the sum of the
coordinate characters, in the convention for equivariant line bundles used here. The identity
−KB = rL therefore gives r ≡ i bi (mod m), proving Equation (4.10).
                                ∑

Lemma 4.5 (Log-concavity and a barycenter half-space bound). A nonzero mean-zero linear
combination of independent mean-one exponentials has a positive continuous log-concave
density on the whole real line. Adding further independent scaled exponentials, with either
sign of coefficient, preserves these properties. If Z has such a density, then
                                         1                  1
                                           ≤ P(Z ≤ EZ) ≤ 1 − .                             (4.24)
                                         e                  e
Proof. The preservation of log-concavity under convolution is a special case of the classical
theory of Prékopa [45, Theorems 7–8]; we give the elementary exponential-specific argument
needed here. A nonzero coefficient vector with sum zero has a positive and a negative
coefficient. The difference aE − bE ′ for a, b > 0 has density
                                                       {
                                            1             ex/b ,   x ≤ 0,
                                    p(x) =                  −x/a
                                           a+b            e      , x ≥ 0.

It is positive, continuous, and log-concave.

same argument with r(x + t)/r(x) shows that T (x) = x∞ r(y)dy is log-concave: T /r is

The integrands are exponential tilts of p, hence log-concave, and the appropriate one-sided
integrals are finite. The preceding argument proves log-concavity of the new densities.
Positivity and continuity are immediate from the displayed formulas. Induction starting with
aE − bE ′ proves the assertions about finite exponential sums, and translation does not affect
them.
    For completeness, Equation (4.24) is the one-dimensional log-concave form of Grünbaum’s
centroid inequality [15]; see [37, Lemma 5.4] and [40, Section 3]. It follows directly here from
the same integral argument. If G is the distribution function of Z, both G and 1 − G are
log-concave. Since G(Z) is uniform on (0, 1), Jensen’s inequality gives
                                                            ∫ 1
                         log G(EZ) ≥ E log G(Z) =                 log t dt = −1.
                                                             0

Applying the same reasoning to 1 − G gives log(1 − G(EZ)) ≥ −1. All the means in the
present application are finite, and both logarithmic expectations just used equal −1. These
two inequalities give Equation (4.24).

Lemma 4.6 (Strict single crossing). Let Z have a positive log-concave probability density on
R, and let E be an independent mean-one exponential. If

                                           Ek(Z + c∗ E) = 0,

then Ek(Z + cE) > 0 for every c < c∗ and Ek(Z + cE) < 0 for every c > c∗ .
Proof. Write p for the density of Z and first consider
                                                  ∫ ∞
                        ψ(t) = Ek(Z + t) =               (1 − y)e−y p(y − t)dy.
                                                    0

This is continuous, by continuity of translation in L1 and boundedness of k. A positive
log-concave density has a continuous representative whose logarithm is finite and concave.
For t1 < t2 , the ratio
                                r(y) = p(y − t2 )/p(y − t1 )
is nondecreasing in y. If ψ(t1 ) = 0, subtraction of the constant r(1) gives
                                    ∫ ∞
                       ψ(t2 ) =           k(y)p(y − t1 )(r(y) − r(1))dy ≤ 0 :
                                    0

the integrand is nonpositive on both (0, 1) and (1, ∞). Equality would force r to be constant
on (0, ∞), by positivity and continuity. Thus log p would have constant increments across

                                                    25
the fixed interval length t2 − t1 on a half-line. Concavity forces it to be affine there: its
almost-everywhere derivative is nonincreasing, and equality of this derivative across a fixed
shift makes it constant on that half-line. Integrability then gives p(y − t1 ) = Ae−λy for y > 0,
with A, λ > 0. But
                                    ∫ ∞
                                                                    Aλ
                       ψ(t1 ) = A         (1 − y)e−(1+λ)y dy =            > 0,
                                    0                            (1 + λ)2

a contradiction. Hence the inequality is strict. Reversing the likelihood-ratio comparison
proves strict positivity to the left of a zero. Continuity shows that ψ either has one strict sign
everywhere or has exactly one zero, with positive sign to its left and negative sign to its right.
   Now put F (c) = Eψ(cE). For c ̸= 0, the density of cE is

                                     qc (t) = |c|−1 e−t/c 1{tc>0} .

If c1 < c2 have the same sign, then on their common support

                               qc2 (t)   |c1 |    (                )
                                       =       exp t(1/c1 − 1/c2 )
                               qc1 (t)   |c2 |

is strictly increasing in t. This holds on the negative half-line as well as on the positive
half-line. If F (c∗ ) = 0 and c∗ ̸= 0, then ψ must have its strict crossing inside that half-line.
Subtracting the likelihood ratio at this crossing proves strict positivity of F (c) for c < c∗ and
strict negativity for c > c∗ within the same parameter half-line.
    The comparisons across zero are also strict. If c∗ > 0, the crossing of ψ lies in (0, ∞),
so ψ > 0 on (−∞, 0] and F (c) > 0 for c ≤ 0. If c∗ < 0, the crossing lies in (−∞, 0), giving
F (c) < 0 for c ≥ 0. Finally F (0) = ψ(0); a zero there gives the two required signs directly
from those of ψ. This proves the assertion for all real parameters.

Lemma 4.7 (Finite critical points). Fix u > 0 and N ≥ 2. Every nonzero finite local

Proof. Equivalently consider a local minimum of Eh(Y ), where Y = u + i ai Xi . At a
nonzero coefficient vector, Lemma 4.5 supplies a continuous positive log-concave density for
Y . First and second differentiation under the expectation are justified by boundedness of h′ ,
its global Lipschitz property, the finite second moments of the variables Xi , and the absence
of an atom at Y = 0. Stationarity in the direction ei − ej gives

                       0 = E[(Xi − Xj )h′ (Y )] = (ai − aj )E[Xi Xj k(Y )].                (4.26)

To see the second equality, condition on all other variables and on S = Xi + Xj . Given S = s,
Xi is uniform on [0, s] and Xj = s − Xi . Integration by parts with x(s − x), whose endpoint
values vanish and whose derivative is s − 2x, gives exactly Equation (4.26).
    For distinct indices, weighting by Xi Xj changes those two independent exponential laws
into independent Gamma(2, 1) laws. Since EXi Xj = 1, no normalization factor appears.
Thus
                            E[Xi Xj k(Y )] = Ek(Y + ai E ′ + aj E ′′ ),                 (4.27)


                                                    26
where the added exponentials are independent of all variables in Y . If three distinct coefficient
values occurred, fix an index i at one value and choose indices at the other two. Equations
(4.26) and (4.27) would give two distinct zeros of

                                  c 7−→ Ek(Y + ai E ′ + cE ′′ ).

Its base variable has a positive full-support log-concave density by Lemma 4.5, contradicting
Lemma 4.6. Therefore there are at most two coefficient values.
    Suppose the two values are b < c and the higher value occurs at indices i ̸= j. A high-low
pair gives a zero at b of d 7→ Ek(Y + cE ′ + dE ′′ ). Strict single crossing makes its value at c
negative. By Equation (4.27), this says E[Xi Xj k(Y )] < 0. As ai = aj , Y depends on this
pair only through S, and

                     E[(Xi − Xj )2 | S] = S 2 /3,       E[Xi Xj | S] = S 2 /6.

Consequently the Hessian in the permissible splitting direction is

                           E[(Xi − Xj )2 k(Y )] = 2E[Xi Xj k(Y )] < 0,

contradicting a minimum. The higher value therefore occurs once. The sum-zero constraint
forces it to be positive and gives Equation (4.25).

    The preceding lemmas leave only one possible shape for a finite nonzero optimizer. To
obtain a bound uniform in the dimension, it remains to control escape to infinity and then
solve the resulting one-variable maximization.

For the second branch, split the exponential integral at X1 = 1 − u/t; above that point
