4.4    Interiority of the canonical vector
Theorem 4.8 (Canonical interior point). For every sufficiently large grading in the subse-
quence under consideration,

                    c0 = (r, 1) ∈ int K        in the original degree coordinates.                (4.30)

Equivalently, f (1) < N . For an exact minimizing rational grading with m ≥ r/N , the
conclusion holds without passage to a limit.

Proof. Suppose that f (1) ≥ N . At the interior point 1 of the exponent orthant, choose a
subgradient p of f . Positive homogeneity gives p · 1 = f (1) and f (x) ≥ p · x on the orthant.
Therefore B0 (x) ≥ (p − 1) · x, and the coefficient sum of p − 1 is nonnegative. Subtracting
the same nonnegative number from each coefficient gives a vector a with sum zero and

                                    B0 (x) ≥ a · x           (x ∈ RN
                                                                   ≥0 ).                          (4.31)

   Take u = 4/3. Applying Equation (4.21) pointwise to Equation (4.31), and using
Lemma 4.3, gives

                                                          1 + B0 (X) −B0 (X)
                                               [(                    )         ]
                          (1 − ην /u)H ≤ E          1+               e
                                                              u
                                              eu
                                          ≤      Eg(u + a · X) ≤ C∗ < 2.
                                              u
All expectations are finite by Equation (4.8). But H ≥ 2/s ≥ 2, so the displayed inequality
is impossible once ην is sufficiently small. Hence f (1) < N for all sufficiently large gradings.
At an exact minimizing rational grading, ην = 0 gives the contradiction immediately.
    The scaled coordinates of c0 are (N, 1), and 1 is interior to the exponent orthant. The
strict epigraph inequality is therefore precisely Equation (4.30). Its membership in the lattice
was already proved in Proposition 4.1.


5     Adjoint jets and the saturated semigroup
We retain the orbifold and jet data of Proposition 4.1. In particular, B is a smooth effective
proper complex orbifold of dimension N , its coarse space is projective, L is an ample orbifold
line bundle, and −KB = rL. At the chosen point the stabilizer is µm , the fiber character
of L is faithful, and equivariant transverse parameters z1 , . . . , zN have characters b1 , . . . , bN .
We use the original, unscaled degree coordinate:
                    {                                                    }
                                                ∑
                                      N
               Λ=     (j, γ) ∈ Z × Z      :j≡        bi γi    (mod m) ,      c0 = (r, 1).
                                                 i

The semigroup Γ records the total-degree-then-lexicographic Taylor initials of sections of jL,
and K is its closed real cone. It has full dimension, contains the positive constant ray, and
has bounded slices of bounded original degree. Its projection onto the exponent coordinates
is the nonnegative orthant. The canonical character identity gives c0 ∈ Λ.
    The adjoint lifting statement below uses these data but does not assume that c0 itself lies
in the interior of K. We use Theorem 4.8 only after proving that statement.




                                                     29
5.1   Vanishing on the smooth orbifold models
We first record the precise form of vanishing needed on a weighted blowup and its resolution.
Divisors and line bundles on a stack are written additively. Nefness and bigness of their
rational classes are understood on the projective coarse space.

Lemma 5.1 (Orbifold vanishing). Let X be a smooth proper Deligne–Mumford stack over
C, with trivial generic stabilizer and projective coarse space. Let Θ be an effective rational
divisor with simple normal crossing support and coefficients less than one. If D is a Cartier
divisor and D − (KX + Θ) is nef and big, then

                                H q (X , OX (D)) = 0     (q > 0).

Proof. Let q : X → X be the coarse morphism. For a prime divisor B ⊂ X, let eB be the
stabilizer order at the generic point of its inverse image. A rational divisor A on X has a
coarse rational divisor Ac , characterized in codimension one by q ∗ Ac = A. Locally the coarse
map is given in the normal direction by t = z eB , so

                        KX = q ∗ (KX + R),
                                                         ∑
                                                    R=       (1 − 1/eB )B.
                                                         B

Only divisors with eB > 1 contribute to R.
   The coefficient of Dc at B is an integral multiple of 1/eB . Consequently

                                      ∆ = R + Θc − {Dc }                                    (5.1)

is effective: the fractional coefficient being subtracted is at most (eB − 1)/eB . The pair (X, ∆)
is klt. Indeed, on a smooth finite quotient uniformizer U → X, the log pullback of ∆ is the
pullback of Θ minus the effective pullback of {Dc }. This boundary is bounded above by the
simple normal crossing boundary Θ|U with coefficients less than one. All its log discrepancies
are therefore positive. The finite-map discrepancy formula, with ramification included in the
displayed canonical identity, gives the same positivity downstairs.
     Normal extension from codimension one identifies

                                    q∗ OX (D) = OX (⌊Dc ⌋).

For completeness, on a finite quotient chart the pushforward is the invariant part of an
invertible module on a normal smooth scheme. Sections extend across sets of codimension at
least two there and then remain invariant, so this pushforward is the rank-one reflexive sheaf
prescribed by its codimension-one orders. Those orders are exactly ⌊Dc ⌋. Taking invariants
is exact in characteristic zero, which also gives

                             H q (X , OX (D)) = H q (X, OX (⌊Dc ⌋)).

    The coarse space has quotient singularities and is locally Q-factorial. Thus ⌊Dc ⌋ is an
integral Q-Cartier Weil divisor. By Equation (5.1),

                          ⌊Dc ⌋ − (KX + ∆) = Dc − (KX + R + Θc ),

which is the nef and big class descended from D − (KX + Θ). Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing
for a klt pair and an integral Q-Cartier Weil divisor now applies [12]. It gives the claimed
vanishing. This argument requires neither flatness of the coarse morphism nor ampleness in
place of nefness and bigness.



                                               30
5.2    The adjoint lifting implication
Lemma 5.2 (Adjoint lattice points). For the orbifold jet data above,

                     (j, α) ∈ Λ,       (j, α) + c0 ∈ int K     =⇒      (j, α) ∈ Γ.                 (5.2)

Proof. The coordinate inequalities of K imply αi + 1 > 0. Since αi is integral, αi ≥ 0. The
bounded-slice property and the positivity of the degree coordinate on K \ {0} give j + r > 0.
Choose a rational number

                      0 < j0 < j + r     such that     p = (j0 , α + 1) ∈ int K.

We construct a section of jL with the required Taylor initial.

Replacing finitely many initials by scalar weights. There are finitely many sections
whose initial indices span a polyhedral cone containing p in its interior. To see this without
assuming finite generation of Γ, choose a small simplex around p inside K and approximate its
vertices by points in the cone generated by Γ. Sufficiently close approximations still surround
p, and each uses only finitely many semigroup elements. The union of those finite lists has
the desired property.
    For this list of sections, choose positive primitive integral weights u1 , . . . , uN such that
scalar u-order has exactly their specified Taylor initials, each as a single monomial. Here is the
finite-order justification. Let d exceed the total degrees of those initials and the total degree
of α. Weights sufficiently close to a common positive value preserve all strict total-degree
comparisons through degree d and place every monomial of total degree greater than d above
the relevant initials. Among monomials of equal degree at most d, successive sufficiently
small rational perturbations of the weights realize the chosen lexicographic order. There are
only finitely many such comparisons. We can include all monomials preceding α among them,
and then clear denominators and divide by the common divisor. Thus, in addition,

                               γ precedes α      =⇒      u · γ < u · α.                            (5.3)

This handles formal Taylor series as well as polynomial expansions, since positivity of the
weights excludes all sufficiently high total degrees at once.
   Set                                                          ∑
                         p0 = u · α,     U = u · (α + 1) = p0 +   ui .
                                                                          i

The affine plane given by original degree j0 and scalar cost U meets the finite cone just chosen
in a relative neighborhood of p. Choose finitely many rational points in that neighborhood
surrounding p in the plane. Their expressions as nonnegative combinations of the integral
cone generators can be taken rational. Clear all denominators simultaneously. Multiplication
of the corresponding sections then gives a positive integer a and sections s1 , . . . , st of aj0 L
                          (1)           (t)
with single u-initials z β , . . . , z β , after rescaling, such that

         u · β (k) = aU,     α + 1 ∈ relint conv{β (1) /a, . . . , β (t) /a} ⊂ {x : u · x = U }.   (5.4)

The relative interior here contains a neighborhood in the entire displayed affine plane. Products
preserve single initials, so no claim about generation of the full section ring has entered this
construction.

parameter system defines every Ik , so these ideals form a multiplicative filtration, including
after passage to the completed Taylor ring.

Multiplier-ideal membership on the exceptional divisor. The congruence (j, α) ∈ Λ

                                        (                                )

   On the chart where xk ̸= 0, pass to the smooth finite uniformizer that sets xk = 1. More

                            Hk = {(ρ, ζ) ∈ Gm × µm : ρuk ζ bk = 1}.

This is a finite extension of µm by µuk , acting on the remaining coordinates by xi 7→ ρui ζ bi xi .

by the defining relation of Hk and the congruence for α. There are no fractional exponents:

    The monomial multiplier-ideal formula says that xν belongs to J (I c ) precisely when ν + 1
is in the interior of c times the Newton polyhedron of I [17]. Its hypotheses hold on this
smooth affine chart. Applying it with c = 1/a proves the claimed membership on every
uniformizer. The ideal and the section are equivariant, so these memberships descend and

assumed.

Adjoint vanishing and restriction. We apply the positivity in Equation (5.6) on a
projective log resolution σ : Y → Z of E and b, isomorphic at the generic point of E. We use
smooth stacks throughout: functorial log resolution in smooth etale charts [23, Theorems 35–
36] descends. Arrange that the total boundary, including the strict transform Ẽ, has simple
normal crossings, and that the restricted morphism τ : Ẽ → E resolves b|E . Write

                                        bOY = OY (−G0 ).

The effective divisor G0 does not contain Ẽ, and σ ∗ H0 − G0 is globally generated by the
pulled-back sections.
    Consider the integral line bundle divisor

                           AY = KY + σ ∗ (P0 − KZ − E) − ⌊G0 /a⌋.

Its difference from KY + {G0 /a} is
                                                      1
                              (j + r − j0 )σ ∗ π ∗ L + (σ ∗ H0 − G0 ).                        (5.8)
                                                      a


                                                     33
The first term is nef and big and the second is nef. The fractional boundary has simple
normal crossings and coefficients less than one. Lemma 5.1 gives H 1 (Y, OY (AY )) = 0. The
divisor restriction sequence therefore gives a surjection

                           H 0 (Y, AY + Ẽ) −→ H 0 (Ẽ, (AY + Ẽ)|Ẽ ).                      (5.9)

   Adjunction identifies the bundle on the right with
                                                          ⌊         ⌋
                            τ ∗ (P0 |E ) + KẼ − τ ∗ KE − (G0 |Ẽ )/a .                     (5.10)

Here round-down commutes with restriction. Indeed, simple normal crossings of Ẽ + Supp G0
prevents distinct components of G0 from sharing a divisor on Ẽ. If an individual intersection
is disconnected, its coefficient is the same on each component, so the equality still holds.
Moreover G0 |Ẽ is the divisor of the pulled-back restricted ideal. Thus Equation (5.10) is
precisely the bundle in the log-resolution definition of the multiplier ideal appearing in
Equation (5.7). That membership supplies a section of Equation (5.10) whose rational section
is the pullback of z α . Surjectivity in Equation (5.9) lifts it to Y.

Regular pushdown and recovery of the initial. The difference between the lifting
bundle and σ ∗ P0 is
                     KY − σ ∗ KZ − σ ∗ E + Ẽ − ⌊G0 /a⌋.                  (5.11)
The part preceding the last term is effective and exceptional over Z. This can be checked
during a resolution by smooth blowups: a center of codimension c ≥ 2 contributes c − 1, or
c − 2 when contained in the strict transform of E, in addition to pullbacks of already effective
exceptional terms. The same calculation holds in the etale smooth charts. The final term
in Equation (5.11) is the negative of an effective divisor. It follows that the lifted rational
section has no pole along any nonexceptional prime divisor. It pushes down to a regular
section of P0 on the normal stack Z. Its restriction to E agrees generically with z α , and
hence agrees everywhere, since both are regular sections on the integral smooth stack E.
    Finally p0 ≥ 0, so P0 is a subsheaf of π ∗ (jL). Normal extension across the center, or the
local weighted blowup charts, gives π∗ OZ = OB . Pushing down thus produces a section of jL.
The exceptional order and the specified restriction say exactly that its u-initial is z α , with no
term of smaller u-cost. Equation (5.3) then excludes every Taylor monomial preceding α in
the original order. This proves Equation (5.2).

5.3   Integral support forms and saturation
We now use the interior conclusion from the preceding section. The next argument explains
why the adjoint implication forces a polyhedral cone, rather than merely imposing a condition
on facets that might happen to be rational.

Theorem 5.3 (The saturated jet semigroup). Suppose c0 ∈ int K. Then the following
statements hold:
  1. K is a rational polyhedral cone.
  2. Every facet has a primitive nonnegative support form η ∈ Λ∗ satisfying η(c0 ) = 1.
  3. The semigroup and its interior lattice points satisfy

                                 Γ = K ∩ Λ,          int K ∩ Λ = c0 + Γ.                    (5.12)




                                                34
In particular, Γ is a finitely generated saturated affine semigroup with group Λ. These
conclusions apply to every sufficiently far grading and chosen point covered by Theorem 4.8,
including its exact rational case.

Proof. Fix such jet data, with c0 ∈ int K ∩ Λ. Put φ(x) = (r/N )f (x), so the epigraph of φ
uses the original degree coordinate j, rather than D0 = N j/r. On the open positive orthant,
φ is a finite convex function and is locally Lipschitz.

A support at a differentiability point has height one. Let x be a differentiability point
of φ in the positive orthant, and let y = (φ(x), x) ∈ ∂K. Homogeneity gives φ(x) = ∇φ(x) · x.
The unique supporting normal ray at y is therefore generated by

                                   η(j ′ , x′ ) = j ′ − ∇φ(x) · x′ ,

and η(c0 ) > 0. Suppose either that this ray is irrational relative to Λ, or that its primitive
integral generator has value greater than one at c0 . In both cases there exists w ∈ Λ with

                                       −η(c0 ) < η(w) < 0.                                  (5.13)

For an integral primitive form of height at least two, take an element of value −1. For an
irrational ray, the subgroup η(Λ) ⊂ R is dense: any nondense additive subgroup of R is
discrete, and discreteness here would make a positive multiple of η primitive integral. This
proves the assertion in the irrational case as well.
    There are integers kν → ∞ and lattice points lν ∈ Λ such that

                                      eν = lν − kν y −→ 0.                                  (5.14)

This is recurrence of the multiples of y in the compact torus RN +1 /Λ. It also follows directly by
the pigeonhole principle applied to successively finer finite partitions of a lattice fundamental
domain. If the resulting return times stay bounded, one of them is an exact period and its
unbounded multiples give Equation (5.14) instead.
    Now lν + w is outside K for large ν, since its η-value tends to the negative number η(w).
In contrast,
                                                   w + c 0 + eν
                                             (                  )
                          lν + w + c0 = kν y +                    ∈ int K                    (5.15)
                                                       kν
for large ν. To justify this strict inclusion, set v = w + c0 , so η(v) > 0 by Equation (5.13).
Differentiability gives, uniformly for v ′ in a small neighborhood of v,

                            φ(x + tvx′ ) = φ(x) + t∇φ(x) · vx′ + o(t).

Thus the j-coordinate of y + tv ′ exceeds φ(x + tvx′ ) for every sufficiently small positive t; the
exponent coordinates remain positive as well. Apply this with t = 1/kν and v ′ = v + eν to
obtain Equation (5.15). Lemma 5.2, applied to the lattice point lν + w, would then put this
point in Γ ⊂ K, a contradiction. Every supporting ray at a differentiability point therefore
has a primitive integral form of height one at c0 .

Only finitely many support forms occur. Choose ϵ > 0 such that the Euclidean ball of
radius ϵ about c0 is contained in K. If a nonnegative support form has η(c0 ) = 1, testing it
on this ball gives ∥η∥ ≤ 1/ϵ. Since Λ∗ is a lattice, only finitely many primitive integral forms
satisfy this bound. Denote the forms obtained at differentiability points by η1 , . . . , ηt .
    These forms, together with the coordinate inequalities, define K. Indeed, convex functions
are differentiable almost everywhere on their open domain. At any given positive x0 , take

                                                  35
differentiability points xν → x0 . Local Lipschitz continuity bounds their gradients, and
therefore
                            φ(xν ) + ∇φ(xν ) · (x0 − xν ) −→ φ(x0 ).
Each expression is the value at x0 of a supporting linear function. Hence the supports at
these differentiability points recover the epigraph on the positive orthant. Since only the
finite list above occurs, K and

                     K ′ = {(j, x) : xi ≥ 0 for all i, ηa (j, x) ≥ 0 for all a}

agree there. We already have K ⊂ K ′ . Conversely, for q ∈ K ′ , the point q + tc0 lies in K ′
and has positive exponent coordinates whenever t > 0. It is thus in K, and closedness gives
q ∈ K on letting t ↓ 0. This proves K = K ′ and rational polyhedrality.
    The coordinate form (j, x) 7→ xi is primitive on Λ: one can prescribe x = ei and choose j
in the requisite congruence class. Its value on c0 is one. All other defining forms also have
height one. Every facet of the full-dimensional polyhedral cone is cut out by a form from an
irredundant sublist, so its primitive support has the asserted height.

Saturation and the interior translation. If q ∈ K ∩ Λ, then q + c0 ∈ int K: translate
a small ball about c0 by q and use addition in the convex cone. Lemma 5.2 gives q ∈ Γ,
proving the first identity in Equation (5.12). If q ∈ int K ∩ Λ, each primitive facet form takes
a positive integral value on q, hence a value at least one. Since its value on c0 is one, all facet
inequalities hold for q − c0 . Thus q − c0 ∈ K ∩ Λ = Γ. The reverse inclusion c0 + Γ ⊂ int K ∩ Λ
follows from the same ball-translation argument. This proves the second identity.
    Finally, triangulate the rational polyhedral cone into finitely many rational simplicial
cones and choose lattice generators for their rays. A lattice point in any such cone is a
nonnegative integral combination of its ray generators plus a lattice point in their bounded
half-open parallelepiped. There are only finitely many such remainder points. Taking their
union over the triangulation proves finite generation of K ∩ Λ. If a positive integral multiple
of q ∈ Λ lies in this semigroup, then q ∈ K by homogeneity, so q already lies in it; this is
saturation. The group is Λ by Proposition 4.1.


6    Two filtrations and a second stabilizer
Fix one of the gradings and points furnished by Theorem 5.3. We retain the original degree j
and put n = N + 1, with N ≥ 4. Thus S = C[C] is a positively graded normal Gorenstein
domain, its vertex o is singular, and its canonical module has a homogeneous generator of
original degree r. The Taylor semigroup and its lattice satisfy

                 Γ = K ∩ Λ,        int(K) ∩ Λ = c0 + Γ,         c0 = (r, 1, . . . , 1).      (6.1)

Here K is rational polyhedral. We also use the finite Taylor-order bound and the eventual
realization of compatible jets from Proposition 4.1. The only volume hypothesis in this
section is
                                    vol(o, C) ≥ 2N n .
                                     ˆ                                               (6.2)
The first filtration separates total Taylor order from original degree. We then assign positive
cost to the constant Taylor direction as well. The resulting second graded ring has a nontrivial
stabilizer, which will supply the same-dimensional slice in Section 7.




                                                36
6.1    The first associated graded ring
For an original-homogeneous section s ∈ Sj , let T (s) be its total Taylor order at the chosen
orbifold point, computed in the fixed smooth uniformizing chart and local frame. Extend the
filtration by direct sums in original degree, and write

                                                  S = grT S.

Its bidegrees will always mean original degree and T -degree, in that order. If τ is a book-
keeping variable for original degree, then S is the subalgebra of C[τ, z1 , . . . , zN ] consisting of
homogeneous Taylor forms τ j P (z) obtained from sections. Each such form satisfies the stabi-
lizer congruence. Taking its further monomial initial with the fixed lexicographic refinement
gives the algebra C[Γ].
    The saturated monomial algebra will determine normality and the canonical degree of
S. A second consequence of saturation is a section whose Taylor form is the constant τ m .
Inverting that section recovers every compatible Taylor monomial; this will determine the
Hilbert series of its zero fiber and give a basis for the next filtration.
Lemma 6.1 (The Taylor graded ring). The algebra S is finitely generated, normal, Cohen–
Macaulay, and Gorenstein. Its canonical module has a homogeneous generator of bidegree
(r, N ). There is a section v ∈ Sm whose initial v is τ m . In particular T (v) = 0, and

                  S[v −1 ] ≃ C[v, v −1 , u1 , . . . , uN ],    T (ui ) = 1,   T (v) = 0.        (6.3)

The ring D = S/(v) is an equidimensional Cohen–Macaulay Gorenstein ring of dimension N ,
with
                   HilbT D(z) = (1 − z)−N ,    deg ωD = (r − m, N ).               (6.4)
Its T -degree-zero piece is C. A bihomogeneous vector-space basis of D can be lifted to sections
ei ∈ S such that, on putting Ti = T (ei ),

                                               {v a ei : a ∈ N}                                 (6.5)

is a vector-space basis of S, compatible with original degree and T -order. The unique vector
of this basis with a + Ti = 0 is 1.
Proof. We first transfer the structure of the monomial algebra to S. By Equation (6.1), Γ is a
finitely generated normal affine semigroup. Hochster’s theorem makes C[Γ] Cohen–Macaulay,
and the canonical-module formula for normal affine semigroup rings identifies its canonical
module with the monomial ideal of interior lattice points; see [16] and [47, Theorem 6.7 and
its following normal-monoid reformulation]. The second identity in Equation (6.1) makes
this ideal principal, generated in multidegree (r, 1, . . . , 1). Thus its bidegree is (r, N ). The
interior-translation identity, rather than saturation alone, is essential here.
    Choose a finite set of generators of Γ and bihomogeneous lifts in S of their monomials.
We lift generation by degreewise subduction, in the terminology of Khovanskii bases [20,
Algorithm 2.11 and Proposition 2.13]. Subtracting products of the lifts cancels any selected
initial monomial. Within a fixed original degree there are only finitely many Taylor orders, and
within each order only finitely many monomials. Consequently this subtraction terminates
and the chosen lifts generate S.
    The same finite list gives a one-parameter flat monomial degeneration. Choose positive
integral costs on the zi that preserve the selected monomial initial of every one of these finitely
many lifts. Such costs exist by approximating the specified lexicographic refinement on this
finite list. The scalar initial algebra contains C[Γ]. In each original bidegree its dimension is
the dimension of S in that bidegree, which is also the number of the corresponding points

                                                       37
of Γ. The inclusion is therefore an equality in every bidegree. Lifting the generators again,
with the same degreewise terminating subtraction, shows that the extended Rees algebra for
this scalar filtration is finite type. As a subalgebra of a Laurent-polynomial extension it is
torsion-free, hence flat, over its parameter line. Its zero fiber is C[Γ] and its nonzero fibers
are S.
     Write R for this extended Rees algebra and λ for its parameter. It retains original
degree and T -degree, and has the additional scalar filtration grading, with scalar weight −1
on λ. A sufficiently large multiple of original degree minus scalar weight gives a positive
grading on R, including positive degree for λ. At its vertex, the local ring A has a normal
Gorenstein quotient A/(λ). Lifting through the nonzerodivisor λ makes A Cohen–Macaulay
and Gorenstein; for the latter equivalence see [48, Tag 0BJJ].
     The local ring A is also normal. Here is a direct verification using R1 + S2 . It is already
Cohen–Macaulay. Let P be a height-one prime of A. If λ ∈ P , reducedness of A/(λ) makes
AP /(λ) a field, so AP is regular. Otherwise choose Q minimal over (P, λ). Since A is a
local domain essentially of finite type over C, the dimension formula and the principal ideal
theorem give ht Q ≤ 2. The normal ring AQ /(λ) has dimension at most one and is regular.
Lifting a regular system of parameters together with λ shows that AQ is regular, and then so
is its localization AP .
     The normal and Gorenstein loci of Spec R are open, contain its vertex, and are invariant
under the positive grading action. Every orbit contracts to that vertex; hence R is normal
and Gorenstein everywhere. Its generic fiber, a localization of R, is S ⊗C C(λ) and is
normal. Normality descends under this faithfully flat field extension, proving normality of S.
Quotienting R by λ − 1 proves the Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein assertions for S as well.
     Adjunction tracks the canonical bidegree. The parameter λ has original degree and
T -degree both zero, so it contributes no shift in these two degrees. Choose a lift of the central
canonical generator homogeneous also for the scalar grading, with its adjunction shift. Its
cokernel in the canonical module of R is equal to its product by λ. Graded Nakayama for
the positive combined grading therefore makes the cokernel zero. Restriction to λ = 1 forgets
the scalar grading but preserves original degree and T -degree. Thus the canonical generator
of S has bidegree (r, N ).
     We next use the constant Taylor direction to describe S over a polynomial parameter. The
vector (m, 0) lies on the constant ray of K and belongs to Λ. Equation (6.1) provides a section
with this leading index. Rescale its value to obtain v = τ m . Choose integer representatives bi
of the stabilizer characters. Eventual compatible jet separation shows that, after inverting
τ m , every monomial τ j z γ with            ∑
                                        j−      bi γi ∈ mZ
                                             i

occurs. Set ui = τ bi zi in that localization. The displayed congruence expresses each allowed
monomial uniquely as a Laurent power of v times a monomial in the ui . This proves
Equation (6.3), including its T -grading. It also shows directly that there is no residual finite
quotient in a nonzero v fiber.
    For each q ≥ 0, consider the T -degree-q piece of S as a module over C[v]. It is torsion-
free. It is also finite: in each original-degree residue class modulo m, multiplication by v
identifies its pieces with an increasing sequence of subspaces of the finite-dimensional space
of compatible degree-q Taylor forms. These subspaces are eventually the full compatible
space by jet separation. Thus there are only finitely many necessary module generators. This
module is consequently free over the principal ideal domain C[v]. Equation (6.3) shows that
its rank is                               (          )
                                           q+N −1
                                                       .
                                             N −1


                                                 38
Reduction modulo v consequently has exactly this dimension in T -degree q, proving the
Hilbert series in Equation (6.4).
    Since v is a nonzerodivisor in the normal Cohen–Macaulay domain S, its quotient is
equidimensional of dimension N and Cohen–Macaulay. Adjunction makes the quotient
Gorenstein and subtracts (m, 0) from the canonical degree. The Hilbert series shows that the
T -degree-zero piece of D is C.
    It remains to obtain a basis of S compatible with the filtration. Lift a bihomogeneous
basis of D to S. These lifts are a C[v]-basis: generation follows by subtracting modulo v
and descending in original degree, and independence follows by reducing a putative relation
modulo v and successively removing its smallest power. Now lift them through the T -filtration
to original-homogeneous sections ei of the indicated orders Ti . Their products with powers
of v have the just-constructed basis as initials. Terminating cancellation in original degree
proves Equation (6.5). Choose ei = 1 for the sole basis vector of T -degree zero; all other Ti
are positive.

6.2   Canonical forms on extended Rees spaces
We make the discrepancy comparison used for both filtrations explicit. If F is a nonnegative
decreasing multiplicative integral filtration on S, set Fp S = S for p ≤ 0 and use the extended
Rees convention
                                            λ−p Fp S ⊂ S[λ, λ−1 ].
                                        ∑
                                RF =                                                       (6.6)
                                       p∈Z

The filtration action has weight zero on S and weight −1 on λ. In particular, RF /(λ) = grF S
and RF [λ−1 ] = S[λ, λ−1 ]. The inclusion S[λ] ⊂ RF gives a birational morphism Spec RF →
C × A1 .

Lemma 6.2 (Rees discrepancy comparison). Suppose F respects original degree, has finite
length in each original homogeneous piece, and grF S is finitely generated. Suppose also that
X = Spec RF is normal and Gorenstein, and that grF S is Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein
with a canonical generator of bidegree (r, Q). Then RF is finite type and its absolute canonical
module has a homogeneous generator of bidegree (r, Q − 1), which on λ ̸= 0 is

                               ΩX = cλ−Q ΩC ∧ dλ,         c ∈ C∗ .                           (6.7)

For a quasi-monomial valuation V centered on X over λ = 0, put ℓ = V (λ) > 0 and
w = V |C(C) . If w is centered at o, then

                                 AC (w) ≤ AX (V ) + (Q − 1)ℓ.                                (6.8)

The same inequality holds whenever the discrepancies involved are finite and defined by
valuation retractions.

Proof. Lift homogeneous generators of grF S to si ∈ S, of filtration orders pi . Cancellation of
initial forms, terminating within each original degree, shows that RF is generated by λ and
λ−pi si . Indeed, an element of Fp S has an expression as a sum of monomials in the si whose
filtration orders are at least p; multiplication by λ−p then introduces only nonnegative extra
powers of λ. Taking a sufficiently large multiple of original degree minus filtration degree
makes every one of these generators positive, with deg λ = 1.
     Cartier adjunction [48, Tag 0B4A] for the nonzerodivisor λ identifies the reduction of
the canonical module of RF with that of grF S, with the shift coming from dλ. Since λ has
filtration weight −1, a lift of the specified central generator has bidegree (r, Q − 1). This lift
generates the whole canonical module: its cokernel is equal to its product by λ, and a finite

                                               39
module bounded below in the positive combined grading cannot have that property unless it
is zero. As the canonical module is torsion-free of rank one over the domain RF , the resulting
generator is free.
    On λ ̸= 0, both this generator and ΩC ∧ dλ generate the same canonical module. Their
ratio is a unit of S[λ, λ−1 ]. The units of the positively graded domain S are the nonzero
constants, so such a unit is cλa . The filtration weight of ΩC ∧ dλ is −1, and the weight of
the lifted generator is Q − 1. It follows that a = −Q, proving Equation (6.7). Computing on
a common smooth birational model gives

                                 AC×A1 (V ) = AX (V ) + Qℓ.                               (6.9)

This computation uses rational top forms and does not require the Rees morphism itself to
be proper.
   On the other hand,
                                 AC×A1 (V ) ≥ AC (w) + ℓ.                          (6.10)
To see this directly, take any smooth proper birational log model of C used to retract w,
and take its product with the parameter line. Include λ = 0 among the simple-normal-
crossing divisors. The monomial retraction of V on this product has discrepancy equal to the
discrepancy of the corresponding retraction of w plus ℓ. Log discrepancy dominates its value
on each such retraction [18, Corollary 5.4 and Remark 5.6]; taking the supremum over the
models of C proves Equation (6.10). Combining it with Equation (6.9) proves the lemma.

6.3   Reducedness and the second filtration
Lemma 6.3 (Reducedness of the quotient). Under Equation (6.2), D is reduced.
Proof. The T -Rees algebra is finite type by Lemma 6.1 and the generator-lifting argument
in Lemma 6.2. Its nonzero fibers are S, and its central fiber S is normal, Cohen–Macaulay,
and Gorenstein. The regular parameter and these fiber properties imply that the total space
is Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein. It is normal as well: away from the central fiber it is
C × Gm , and at every codimension-one point of the central fiber the quotient by λ is a field.
Thus it is regular in codimension one and satisfies Serre’s condition S2 .
    Let H be an irreducible component of the divisor v = 0 in Spec S, and write ν =
ordH (v) ≥ 1. At its generic point the normal central fiber is a discrete valuation ring. The
total space is therefore regular there, of local dimension two, with parameters λ and a lift t
of a central uniformizer. In this local ring

                                        v = atν + λb

for a unit a and a regular element b. Take the monomial valuation with costs V (λ) = 1 and
V (t) = 1/ν. Its discrepancy on the total space is 1 + 1/ν. For its restriction w to C(C) one
has
                                 w(v) ≥ 1,       w(ei ) ≥ Ti ,
because λ−Ti ei is regular on the Rees space. Hence w(v a ei ) ≥ a + Ti .
    By Lemma 6.1, every nonconstant original-homogeneous basis vector has a strictly positive
lower bound a + Ti . Thus w is centered exactly at o. The series counting the basis with these
costs is
                            z a+Ti = (1 − z)−1 HilbT D(z) = (1 − z)−n .
                        ∑

                        a,i

The vectors of cost below k consequently number k n /n! + O(k n−1 ). They span the valuation
quotient, so
                                        vol(w) ≤ 1.                                    (6.11)

                                              40
These finite-colength quotients of S are supported at o; their lengths agree with those after
localization at the vertex.
    Apply Lemma 6.2 with Q = N and ℓ = 1. It gives

                                      AC (w) ≤ N + 1/ν.

If ν ≥ 2, Equation (6.11) yields

                             vol(o,
                             ˆ      C) ≤ (N + 1/2)N +1 < 2N N +1 .

For the strict inequality, use
                                   1               N +1  5
                                 (         )
                  (N + 1) log 1 +              <        ≤ < log 2,         N ≥ 4.
                                  2N                2N   8
This contradicts Equation (6.2). All the multiplicities of v are therefore one. Its quotient
D is generically reduced, and it is Cohen–Macaulay, hence satisfies S1 . The reducedness
criterion R0 + S1 proves the assertion; see [48, Tag 033P].

   Define a second filtration by assigning the basis in Equation (6.5) the costs

                                          W (v a ei ) = a + Ti                             (6.12)

and taking spans of basis vectors of cost at least the indicated level. Unlike T , this filtration
is positive on every nonconstant original-homogeneous vector.
    There is also a description independent of the lifted basis. Write Tq S = {s : T (s) ≥ q},
with Tq S = S for q ≤ 0. For the distinguished section v fixed above, one has
                                          p
                                          ∑
                                 Wp S =         v a Tp−a S    (p ≥ 0).                     (6.13)
                                          a=0

Indeed, every basis term v b ei on the right has b + Ti ≥ p. Conversely, for such a term choose
a = min{p, b}; then v b−a ei ∈ Tp−a S. Thus changing the compatible lifts ei does not change
W . The multiplicativity of T also makes the right side of Equation (6.13) multiplicative. The
remaining point is to identify the associated graded algebra, not merely its Hilbert function.
Proposition 6.4 (The two-filtration structure). The filtration W is multiplicative, with

                   G = grW S ≃ D[v],               degW v = 1,     degW |D = T.            (6.14)

Here v is a regular polynomial variable of original degree m. Moreover

                        HilbW G(z) = (1 − z)−n ,             deg ωG = (r, n).              (6.15)

The W -Rees space is a finite-type normal Gorenstein variety. Its canonical generator has
bidegree (r, n − 1) and, on λ ̸= 0, is cλ−n ΩC ∧ dλ.
Proof. Expand a product ei ej in the basis v a ek . Compatibility of that basis with total Taylor
initials shows that every nonzero term has Tk ≥ Ti + Tj . Its W -cost a + Tk is therefore at
least Ti + Tj . Terms with equality have precisely a = 0 and Tk = Ti + Tj ; their images are
the product of the images of ei , ej in D = S/(v). Factoring out the displayed powers of v
proves multiplicativity and the algebra isomorphism in Equation (6.14). In particular the
variable v is regular even if D has several components.
    The Hilbert series follows from Equation (6.4). Adjoining the polynomial variable of
bidegree (m, 1) changes the canonical degree (r − m, N ) to (r, n). Thus G is reduced, Cohen–
Macaulay, and Gorenstein. The W -filtration has finite length in fixed original degree, as is

                                                    41
clear from its basis description; lifting finitely many generators of G proves finite generation
of its Rees algebra.
    The nonzero fibers of this Rees family are S, and its central fiber is G. Consequently the
total space is Cohen–Macaulay and Gorenstein. For normality, away from λ = 0 it is C × Gm .
A codimension-one point on λ = 0 is the generic point of a central component. Since G is
reduced, its local ring there is a field, and the total local ring has maximal ideal generated
by the nonzerodivisor λ. It is regular. The total space satisfies R1 and S2 , hence is normal.
Notice that normality of D or of G is not required in this argument. Finally Lemma 6.2,
with Q = n, gives the canonical generator and top-form identity.

Example: the quadratic cone. The two stabilizers and filtrations can already differ for
an ordinary double point. Let
                                                                               N
                                                                               ∑
                     S = C[a, z1 , . . . , zN , b]/(ab − q(z)),       q(z) =         zi2 ,
                                                                               i=1

with all original degrees equal to one. Here r = N and m = 1. At the quotient point
[a : z : b] = [1 : 0 : 0], the chart a = 1 has b = q(z). Taking v = a, the three degrees are

                                                           a zi b
                                    original degree        1      1   1
                                           T               0      1   2
                                          W                1      1   2

The first Taylor graded ring has the same presentation as S, and D = C[z1 , . . . , zN , b]/(q(z)).
The family Spec S → A1t defined by t = v = a has invariant parameter for the T -action.
After inverting t, b = q(z)/a gives the polynomial family of Equation (6.3). With a = λ−1 a,
zi = λ−1 zi , and b = λ−2 b, the second Rees space is

                                       X = {λab − q(z) = 0}.

Its action has weights (−1, 1, 1, 2) on (λ, a, zi , b). The central point with b = 1 and all other
coordinates zero therefore has stabilizer h = 2. Its transverse slice

                                  Y = {b = 1} = {λa − q(z) = 0}

is again an ordinary double point of dimension n = N + 1. Thus the original stabilizer m = 1
and the new stabilizer h = 2 play different roles, and taking this slice preserves the original
dimension.

6.4   A nontrivial stabilizer on the new central ring
Lemma 6.5 (Free gradings and polynomial rings). Let E be a finitely generated positively
graded reduced equidimensional Cohen–Macaulay C-algebra of dimension N ≥ 2, with E0 = C
and Hilb E(z) = (1 − z)−N . If the grading action has trivial stabilizer at every nonvertex
closed point of Spec E, then E is a polynomial ring on N generators of degree one.

Proof. We first justify that weight one defines an honest line bundle on Z = Proj E. Choose
positive homogeneous algebra generators aj , with degrees wj . At a nonvertex closed point q,
its grading stabilizer is
                                       µgcd{wj :aj (q)̸=0} .


                                                   42
By hypothesis this gcd is one. Invert the product f of those active generators. Bézout’s
                                                      ∏ c
identity supplies integers cj with j cj wj = 1, so u = j ajj is an invertible homogeneous
                                  ∑

element of degree one in Ef . Consequently

                                        Ef = (Ef )0 [u, u−1 ].                                 (6.16)

These open sets cover the puncture: they contain all its closed points, and a finite-type
scheme over C is Jacobson. Their degree-zero charts cover Z. Equation (6.16) gives a Zariski
Gm -torsor over Z, and makes LZ = OZ (1) invertible, with OZ (k) = L⊗k         Z . A positive power
of this line bundle is ample by the construction of Proj, so LZ is ample.
     The same charts show that Z is reduced, equidimensional, and Cohen–Macaulay, of
                                                                 −1
dimension N − 1. The Hilbert leading coefficient gives LN      Z    = 1. Each irreducible projective
component has a positive integral degree for this actual ample line bundle. There is therefore
only one component, and reducedness makes Z integral. The image V0 of E1 in H 0 (Z, LZ )
has dimension N : restriction is injective, since a nonzero homogeneous element in a reduced
positive-dimensional equidimensional ring cannot vanish on its whole puncture.
     We construct successive Cartier sections while tracking the images of V0 , not assuming
surjectivity onto full spaces of sections. Suppose Zi is a positive-dimensional integral projective
Cohen–Macaulay scheme obtained after i cuts, and that the image Vi of V0 on it has dimension
N − i. Choose a nonzero section si ∈ Vi . Its zero scheme Zi+1 is an effective Cartier divisor.
It is nonempty, because LZ |Zi is ample of positive degree, and it is pure and Cohen–Macaulay.
Its degree is again one. The component-degree formula forces a single component of generic
multiplicity one; the S1 property then makes this divisor reduced, hence integral. The kernel
of restriction Vi → H 0 (Zi+1 , LZ |Zi+1 ) is exactly Csi : division by si identifies that kernel with
regular global functions on the proper integral scheme Zi , and those functions are constant.
Thus dim Vi+1 = N − i − 1.
     After N − 1 cuts, the resulting scheme is a single reduced point and the remaining image
space has dimension one. Choose a final section nonzero at that point. Lifting all these sections
to E1 gives N elements whose common zero on Proj E is empty. Their ideal is therefore
irrelevant-primary and they form a homogeneous system of parameters. Cohen–Macaulayness
makes the sequence regular. The quotient has Hilbert series

                                     (1 − z)N Hilb E(z) = 1.

It is C, so induction on degree, or graded Nakayama, shows that these N linear elements
generate E. The resulting surjection from a polynomial ring on N degree-one variables is an
isomorphism by the same Hilbert series.

Corollary 6.6 (A nontrivial second stabilizer). There is a nonvertex closed point of Spec D
whose T -grading stabilizer has order h ≥ 2.

Proof. Otherwise Lemma 6.5 would make D a polynomial ring on N degree-one generators,
and Proposition 6.4 would make G a polynomial ring on n = N + 1 generators. Choose these
generators homogeneous also for original degree and lift them to S. Terminating cancellation
in the W -filtration shows that the lifts generate S. A surjection from a polynomial ring on n
variables to the n-dimensional domain S has zero kernel. Thus C would be smooth, contrary
to our standing hypothesis. Stabilizers at nonvertex points of a positive grading are finite, so
the asserted order h ≥ 2 exists.




                                                 43
7     The slice estimate and the supremum bootstrap
Throughout this section, n = N + 1 ≥ 5, and the local theorem is assumed in dimensions
smaller than n. Recall that pn = 2(N/n)n and that Mn is the supremum of d(x, X) over
all singular boundary-zero klt germs of dimension n. The smooth-value upper bound gives
Mn ≤ 1; no bound by pn is assumed. We first work with a fixed singular cone o ∈ C = Spec S
obtained from Proposition 2.5, such that d(o, C) ≥ pn . Its minimizing Reeb vector ξ is
normalized by AC (wtξ ) = n.
    Choose a sufficiently fast grading from Lemma 2.6 in the large-stabilizer range, and
take m = mmax ≥ r/N . All constructions in Proposition 6.4 then apply. We shall use, in
particular,

      S̄ = grT S,        D = S̄/(v̄),            G = grW S = D[v],             HilbG (z) = (1 − z)−n .   (7.1)

Here W (v) = 1, W |D = T , and D has a positive T -grading. The Rees total space X =
Spec ReesW S is normal and Gorenstein. Its parameter λ has action weight −1, and the
action is trivial on S. The central ring G has canonical filtration shift n. We also use the
family Spec S̄ → A1t defined by t = v̄, whose parameter has T -degree zero. Away from t = 0
it has the graded description

                    S̄[v̄ −1 ] ≃ C[v̄, v̄ −1 ][u1 , . . . , uN ],     T (v̄) = 0,   T (ui ) = 1.         (7.2)

The equivariance in Equation (7.2) will be essential below.

7.1    A slice through a point with nontrivial stabilizer
By Corollary 6.6, there is a nonvertex closed point yD ∈ Spec D whose T -grading stabilizer is
µh , with h ≥ 2. Set y = (yD , 0) ∈ Spec D[v], considered as a point of the central fiber of X.
Its stabilizer for the Rees action is the same µh .
Lemma 7.1 (The uniformizing slice and its tests). There is a normal Gorenstein algebraic
germ y ∈ Y of dimension n, preserved by µh , with a nonzero function λY ∈ mY,y of character
−1, such that Y is klt away from λY = 0. Every quasi-monomial valuation u centered at y
gives a quasi-monomial valuation w centered at o ∈ C. Writing ℓ = u(λY ) > 0, one has

                                AC (w) ≤ N ℓ + AY (u),                vol(w) ≤ ℓ−n .                     (7.3)

The comparison is valid before klt at y has been established.
Proof. Choose a positive-W -degree homogeneous function f on X with f (y) ̸= 0. Such a
function exists because yD is not the vertex of the positively graded ring D; lift a nonvanishing
homogeneous function from the central fiber. Write d = W (f ) > 0 and c = f (y). On the
open set U = {f ̸= 0} ⊂ X, take the level slice Y0 = {f = c}. The action map

                                  θ : Y0 × Gm −→ U,                 (q, a) 7−→ a · q,

is finite étale: it is the cover obtained by adjoining a root ad = f /c of an invertible function.
We take the germ of Y0 at y and denote it by Y . Normality and the Gorenstein property
descend from the étale product description, and dim Y = dim X − 1 = n. The subgroup µh
fixes y and preserves the level slice, since h divides d.
     The restriction λY of λ has character −1. It is a nonzero divisor on Y : its pullback to
Y × Gm differs from the pullback of λ only by the invertible group character a−1 . It vanishes
at y. Since Xλ̸=0 ≃ C × Gm is klt, the étale product description also shows that Y is klt
away from λY = 0.

                                                             44
   We record the function-field relation to C. In K(C)(λ) the action fixes K(C) and gives λ
weight −1, so
                    f = λ−d s for some s ∈ S,        λdY = s/c on Y.
After inverting λY , each component of the slice is finite over the open set {s ̸= 0} ⊂ C. It
dominates this open set: the equation is monic in λY , and the resulting finite algebra is flat
over S[s−1 ]. Moreover λY does not vanish identically on any component through y. Thus
K(Y ) is a finite extension of K(C), and S injects into K(Y ).
    Extend u to K(Y )(a) by the Gauss rule with a of value zero and residue transcendental
over the residue field of u. This is the extension trivial on the group factor. Denote by V its
restriction through θ to K(X). Its center is the generic point of the orbit through y, and

                               AX (V ) = AY (u),         V (λ) = ℓ.                       (7.4)

Indeed, on the product a log smooth model defining u may simply be multiplied by Gm ; the
group parameter contributes no discrepancy. Pulling back log smooth models by the finite
étale chart preserves the canonical divisor and discrepancy in the restricted-value scaling.
These assertions do not require u to be µh -invariant.
    Let w = V |K(C) . Since elements of S are invariant under the Rees action, their pullbacks
to Y × Gm are independent of a, and

                                w(s′ ) = u(s′ |Y )       (s′ ∈ S).                        (7.5)

Equivalently, w is the restriction of u along the finite extension K(Y )/K(C). The Ab-
hyankar equality is preserved by finite extension and restriction, so w is quasi-monomial [18,
Proposition 3.7].
   Write F p S = {W ≥ p} for the second filtration. If s′ ∈ F p S, the Rees function λ−p s′ is
regular on X, hence its restriction is regular at y. Therefore

                                          w(s′ ) ≥ pℓ.                                    (7.6)

Since F 1 S is the vertex maximal ideal, this proves that w is centered exactly at o. Applying
Lemma 6.2 with canonical shift Q = n, and then Equation (7.4), gives the discrepancy
inequality in Equation (7.3).
    Finally, Equation (7.1) implies

                                                 pn
                                dimC S/F p S =      + O(pn−1 ).                           (7.7)
                                                 n!
For p = ⌈k/ℓ⌉, Equation (7.6) gives F p S ⊆ ak (w). The valuation ideal has support only at
o, so its colength is the same before and after localizing S at the vertex. Taking leading
coefficients in Equation (7.7) proves vol(w) ≤ ℓ−n .

Lemma 7.2 (The slice is klt). The germ y ∈ Y is klt.

Proof. If it were not klt, there would be a prime divisor E on a log resolution of Y with
AY (E) ≤ 0 and center containing y. By Lemma 7.1, its center is contained in λY = 0, so
a = ordE (λY ) > 0. Choose a log resolution also resolving this function and the ideal of y,
and choose a closed point q of E over y. In local regular parameters at q, give a parameter
defining E cost 1 and the other parameters positive costs tending to zero. The resulting
quasi-monomial valuations uε , centered exactly at y, satisfy

                   AY (uε ) = AY (E) + O(ε),         ℓε = uε (λY ) = a + O(ε).


                                               45
Their restrictions wε are centered at o. Since C is klt, AC (wε ) > 0; hence Equation (7.3)
either already gives a contradiction through a nonpositive upper bound for this discrepancy,
or gives
                                                               AY (uε ) n
                                                         (             )
                      n                      n
                  2N ≤ vol(o, C) ≤ AC (wε ) vol(wε ) ≤ N +
                          ˆ                                               .
                                                                  ℓε
The quantity inside the last power is positive whenever this chain is applicable, and its limit
superior is at most N . Letting ε tend to zero contradicts 2N n > N n .

Lemma 7.3 (Singularity of the slice). The germ y ∈ Y is singular.

Proof. Suppose that Y were smooth at y. The étale product chart then implies that X is
smooth at the corresponding point. In its regular local ring, λ is an eigenfunction of character
−1 for µh . Lift the product parameter v ∈ G = D[v] equivariantly to a function ṽ of character
1. Its differential is nonzero: the class of v is nonzero in the cotangent space of Spec G at
(yD , 0), which is a quotient of the cotangent space of X.
    Consequently H = {ṽ = 0} ⊂ X is smooth at y, and the germ of Spec D at yD is the
hypersurface cut out in H by λ|H . This is a nonzero equation: λ and ṽ form a regular
sequence because v is regular in G. If λ|H has a nonzero linear part, D is smooth at yD .
Otherwise it is a minimal hypersurface equation whose character is −1 (mod h), and this
character is nontrivial.
    We now use the other deformation S̄ over t = v̄. Its special fiber is D, and t is invariant
under the T -action and therefore under µh . Complete its local ring at the point yD of the
special fiber. The completion is flat over C[[t]]. Choose a minimal system of eigen-coordinates
of the completed local ring of D and lift them equivariantly. Complete Nakayama gives a
surjection
                               P = C[[t, x1 , . . . , xe ]] −→ ÔSpec S̄,yD
with kernel I, where t is fixed and every xi is an eigen-coordinate. Flatness identifies I/tI
with the kernel of the special-fiber presentation.
   If D is smooth at yD , this kernel is zero and Nakayama gives I = 0. In the other case it is
generated by the minimal hypersurface relation of character −1. Lift that generator to I and
average it to its character to obtain a relation F̃ of character −1. Nakayama gives I = (F̃ ).
Because the base parameter is invariant and −1 is a nontrivial character, one has

                                      F̃ (t, 0, . . . , 0) = 0.

In both cases, substituting x1 = · · · = xe = 0 defines a µh -fixed formal section over C[[t]]
through yD .
    Since yD is not the vertex, there is a positive-T -degree homogeneous element of D nonzero
at yD . Lift it homogeneously to S̄. Its value on the formal section is a unit, so remains
nonzero after passing to C((t)). On the other hand, Equation (7.2) identifies this generic
fiber, with its µh -action, with standard affine N -space: each coordinate has character 1. For
h ≥ 2 its fixed-point scheme is exactly the origin, where every positive-T -degree function
vanishes. This is the required contradiction.

7.2   The character contribution to colength
By Lemma 7.2, a minimizing valuation u∗ exists at y ∈ Y and is quasi-monomial [52,
Theorem 1.2(1)]. It is invariant under µh : this follows from uniqueness up to scaling and
invariance of log discrepancy under automorphisms, or directly from [51, Theorem 1.1 and
Corollary 1.2]. Write
                  A′ = AY (u∗ ),     ℓ = u∗ (λY ) > 0,     σ = vol(u∗ ) > 0,
and let w be the valuation of C constructed in Lemma 7.1.
Lemma 7.4 (Equal leading character lengths). Let R = OY,y and let at = {g ∈ R : u∗ (g) ≥ t}.
For every character χ ∈ Z/hZ,
                                          σ n

Proof. The valuation ideals are µh -invariant, so these character quotients are defined. Multi-

                           (R/at−jℓ )χ ,−→ (R/at )χ−j       (j ≥ 0).
Indeed, the value of a product is the sum of the values, so the kernel is exactly the indicated
valuation cutoff. For any two characters one may choose 0 ≤ j ≤ h − 1 connecting them.
With H0 = (h − 1)ℓ, this gives, for each fixed χ,
                   length(R/at−H0 ) ≤ h dimC (R/at )χ ≤ length(R/at+H0 ).
The total length has asymptotic σtn /n! + o(tn ), proving the assertion. The argument uses the
primitive character of the nonzero function λY , and requires no assumption on the tangent
representation.

7.3   The upper bound without a same-dimensional assumption
Theorem 7.7 (The upper bound). Assume the local ODP volume theorem in all dimensions
smaller than n. Then Mn ≤ pn . Equivalently, every singular boundary-zero klt n-dimensional
germ satisfies
                                 vol(x,
                                 ˆ      X) ≤ 2(n − 1)n .
Proof. Suppose Mn > pn . Choose singular klt germs whose densities di > pn tend to Mn .
Proposition 2.5 gives for each of them a singular Gorenstein K-polystable cone oi ∈ Ci ,
smooth off the vertex, with the same density di .
    Fix i and choose the fast gradings of Lemma 2.6 for this cone. If mmax ≤ r/N holds along
an infinite subsequence, Theorem 3.1 implies that Ci is smooth or the standard ODP cone.
The first possibility contradicts its singularity. The second contradicts di > pn , since the
normalized volume at an ODP is 2(n − 1)n by Lemma 2.3. Thus the large-stabilizer condition
holds for all sufficiently far terms. Applying Lemma 7.6 to one such term gives
                                                 di ≤ pn /2 + Mn /2.
Letting i tend to infinity yields Mn ≤ pn /2 + Mn /2, contrary to Mn > pn .
   All choices of sufficiently fast gradings in this argument are made separately for each fixed
cone Ci . Neither an attained supremum nor approximation estimates uniform over different
cones are required. The slice bound used only the definition of Mn , so the argument assumes
no same-dimensional ODP estimate.

                                                         48
7.4    Equality, a strict count, and the maximal stabilizer
Suppose now that the fixed cone satisfies d(o, C) = pn . Theorem 7.7 is available. For
every sufficiently fast grading in the large-stabilizer range, take m = mmax and make the
construction above.

Lemma 7.8 (Consequences of equality). One has h = 2, d(y, Y ) = pn , and A′ = N ℓ. After
rescaling u∗ so that ℓ = 1, the resulting restriction w satisfies
                                                                             2N
      A′ = N,      σ = 2,      AC (w) = 2N,         vol(w) = 2−N ,     w=       wtξ .      (7.15)
                                                                              n
The optimal splitting fraction in Equation (7.8) is x = 1/2, and all inequalities producing that
estimate are equalities at the level of leading coefficients.

Proof. The left endpoint of Equations (7.11)–(7.12) is now pn , and the right endpoint is at
most pn . Every inequality is therefore an equality. In particular,

                                  h = 2,      (A′ )n σ = 2N n .

Combining this with Equation (7.13) gives

                                 N N = (A′ )N ℓ σ/2 = N n ℓ/A′ ,

so A′ = N ℓ. Rescaling u∗ by ℓ−1 makes ℓ = 1, hence A′ = N and σ = 2. Equation (7.14)
then gives x = 1/2 and the refined volume bound becomes vol(w) ≤ 2−N . The discrepancy
bound becomes AC (w) ≤ 2N .
   Since w is an admissible centered valuation,

                          vol(o, C) ≤ AC (w)n vol(w) ≤ (2N )n 2−N = 2N n .
                   2N n = ˆ

Both factors are positive. Thus both displayed upper bounds are attained, and w computes
the normalized volume minimum. Uniqueness up to scaling [51, Theorem 1.1], together with
AC (wtξ ) = n, gives the last identity in Equation (7.15).

Lemma 7.9 (The distinguished section cannot have value greater than two). In the nor-
malization of Lemma 7.8, the section v ∈ Sm used to define the two filtrations satisfies
w(v) ≤ 2.

Proof. Suppose w(v) > 2. Choose a fixed real number t with
                                          1      1
                                              <t< ,
                                         w(v)    2

and set ak = ⌈tk⌉ and pk = ⌊k/2⌋. For large k one has pk − ak > 0. Use the vector-space
basis v b ei supplied by Lemma 6.1; it is adapted to W , with W (v b ei ) = b + Ti . Let Ek be the
span of its basis vectors with level less than pk − ak .
     Multiplication by v ak maps Ek injectively into S/F pk S. To see injectivity modulo this
filtration, the initial form of v is the regular polynomial variable v in G = D[v]. Hence
multiplication by v ak raises every nonzero initial level by exactly ak and kills no initial form.
Moreover, every element of v ak Ek has w-value greater than k: w is nonnegative on S and
ak w(v) > k.
     Thus the kernel of
                                  S/F pk S −→ S/(F pk S + ak )

                                                         (1/2 − t)n n

This is a strict positive leading-order loss in the first term of the exact splitting Equation (7.9).
The second term still satisfies the character estimate in Equation (7.10). At x = 1/2, ℓ = 1,
and σ/h = 1, these estimates give

                             vol(w) ≤ 2−n + 2−n − (1/2 − t)n < 2−N ,

contradicting Lemma 7.8. Only the single exponent ak is used at each cutoff, so there is no
overlap between collections of powers to count.

Lemma 7.10 (Rounding the maximal stabilizer). Along the fast gradings of the fixed equality
cone, the large-stabilizer construction implies N mmax ≤ r for every sufficiently far term.
Proof. Choose fixed torus eigen-generators g1 , . . . , gq of S, with characters χ1 , . . . , χq . Write
                                         r
                                    ζ=     ξ + ε,        ∥ε∥ −→ 0.
                                         n
The ξ-weights of the generators are positive. Consequently there are fixed constants c1 , c2 > 0
such that their ζ-degrees lie between c1 r and c2 r for all sufficiently far gradings. Also
m = mmax ≤ maxi degζ gi = O(r), by Lemma 2.6.
    The section v ∈ Sm has a polynomial lift in these generators homogeneous for ζ. Every
monomial in such a lift uses a bounded number of generators, because its degree is m = O(r)
and each generator degree is at least c1 r. Its possible torus characters therefore belong to a
fixed finite set, independent of the grading and of the chosen section v. If χ is any character
occurring nontrivially in v, then
                                                    r
                                   m = ⟨ζ, χ⟩ =       ⟨ξ, χ⟩ + ⟨ε, χ⟩,

and hence, uniformly for these characters,
                                                nm
                                     ⟨ξ, χ⟩ =      + O(∥ε∥/r).
                                                 r
Taking the minimum over the nonzero character components of v is precisely wtξ (v); the
same estimate therefore holds even when v is not itself a torus eigenfunction. Lemma 7.8
gives
                                   2N m               2N m
                          w(v) =         + O(∥ε∥/r) =        + o(1/r).                    (7.16)
                                     r                   r
By Lemma 7.9, w(v) ≤ 2. Thus N m − r ≤ O(∥ε∥) = o(1). The left side is an integer, so it is
nonpositive for all sufficiently far terms. On an exact rational ray the error is zero, and the
same conclusion is immediate. All constants here concern the fixed cone C only.

Theorem 7.11 (The equality cone). If a singular cone obtained in Proposition 2.5 satisfies
d(o, C) = pn , then it is the standard ordinary double point cone.
Proof. Take the fast primitive gradings of Lemma 2.6. A term either already has N mmax ≤ r,
or lies in the large-stabilizer range. In the latter range, all constructions above are available
for sufficiently far terms, and Lemma 7.10 again gives N mmax ≤ r. The entire sequence
therefore eventually satisfies the small-stabilizer hypothesis. Theorem 3.1 identifies C with
the smooth affine cone or the standard quadratic cone. Since o ∈ C is singular, only the
ordinary double point remains.

8     Equality at the original germ and global consequences
We complete the return from the cone to the original singularity. The lci case of the gap
theorem is already known [34, Theorem 1.3]. We include the hypersurface argument needed
here, so that the source of strictness in the equality case is explicit.

8.1   A weighted hypersurface bound
Lemma 8.1 (A hypersurface test). Let x ∈ X be a klt hypersurface germ of dimension
n, with equation F in regular ambient parameters z0 , . . . , zn . For positive rational weights
w0 , . . . , wn , write dF for the weighted order of F . Then
                                                       (∑n                   )n

therefore assume that they are positive integers. Choose a positive common multiple D1 of
the wi , and in OX,x put
                                        D /w

                                                       51
Proposition 8.2 (Hypersurface equality). If x ∈ X is a singular klt hypersurface germ of
dimension n ≥ 2, then
                               vol(x,
                               ˆ      X) ≤ 2(n − 1)n .
If equality holds, the quadratic part of a local equation is nondegenerate, and (X, x) is
analytically an ordinary double point.

Proof. Let q = multx (F ) ≥ 2. Weights all equal to one in Lemma 8.1 give

                                  vol(x,
                                  ˆ      X) ≤ q(n + 1 − q)n ,

and klt implies q < n + 1. The function b(t) = t(n + 1 − t)n satisfies

                 b′ (t) = (n + 1)(1 − t)(n + 1 − t)n−1 < 0   (1 < t < n + 1).

Thus q > 2 gives a strict bound below 2(n − 1)n .
    Suppose q = 2 and the quadratic part is degenerate. After a linear change of coordinates,
choose a direction absent from the quadratic part. Give it weight 1 − ϵ, and give every other
direction weight one, where 0 < ϵ < 1/3 is rational. Every term of ordinary degree at least
three has weight greater than two, so dF = 2. The bound becomes

                                        2(n − 1 − ϵ)n
                                                      .
                                            1−ϵ
Its logarithmic derivative at ϵ = 0 is −n/(n − 1) + 1 = −1/(n − 1) < 0. It is therefore strictly
smaller than 2(n − 1)n for sufficiently small ϵ > 0. Equality forces a nondegenerate quadratic
part, and the holomorphic Morse Lemma gives the asserted analytic germ.

8.2   Completion of the induction
Proof of Theorem 1.1. The cases n = 2, 3, 4 were established in Section 2, the last by Theo-
rem 2.4. Suppose the theorem is known in lower dimensions and let n = N + 1 ≥ 5. The
supremum argument of Theorem 7.7 gives Mn ≤ pn , hence the asserted inequality for every
singular germ.
    Now suppose d(x, X) = pn . Apply Proposition 2.5 to obtain a K-polystable cone C with
the same density and edim(X, x) ≤ edim(C, o). The equality argument of Theorem 7.11
makes C an ordinary double point. Therefore edim(X, x) ≤ n + 1.
    Since x is singular, its embedding dimension is exactly n + 1, and it is a hypersurface
germ. To see this algebraically, start with an embedding in a smooth ambient variety and
use equations with independent linear parts to cut the ambient germ down to dimension
n + 1. The remaining ideal is a height-one prime in a regular local ring, so is principal.
Proposition 8.2 shows that its equation has nondegenerate quadratic part and hence that the
analytic germ is ODP.
    Conversely, Lemma 2.3 gives equality at every analytic ODP. This proves both directions
of the equality statement and completes the induction.

8.3   The global comparison
Proof of Corollary 1.2. For every closed point x of a K-semistable Q-Fano n-fold V , the
local-to-global comparison gives
                                                       )n
                                                 n+1
                                             (
                               (−KV )n ≤                    vol(x,
                                                            ˆ      V ).
                                                  n
This follows from [33, Theorem 21]; K-semistability and Ding semistability agree in this
setting by [33, Theorem 13(2)]. If V is singular, apply Theorem 1.1 at a singular closed point:
                                        )n                    (           )n
                                  n+1                     n2 − 1
                              (
                                                       n
                          n
                   (−KV ) ≤                  2(n − 1) = 2                      < 2nn .
                                   n                        n

    If V is smooth and V ∼ ̸= Pn , the theorem of Li–Miao gives (−KV )n ≤ 2nn ; its equality
cases are a smooth quadric and P1 × Pn−1 [28, Theorem 1.1]. Both have Kähler–Einstein
metrics, given by the homogeneous quadric metric and the suitably scaled Fubini–Study
product metric, respectively. They are therefore K-polystable [3, Theorem 1.1]. Their degrees
are
            (−KQn )n = (nH)n = 2nn ,        (−KP1 ×Pn−1 )n = (2H1 + nH2 )n = 2nn .
For n = 2, a smooth quadric surface is P1 × P1 . The strict singular bound excludes every
other equality case.
